areas.title: Military service
areas.intro: The new military service law in force since 1 January 2026.
areas.publishers: Federal agencies, the Bundeswehr and town halls

topics.title: Length of voluntary service
topics.law: For new FWD entrants from 1 January 2026, the ordinary commitment is six to eleven months. Soldiers already serving on 31 December 2025 have a statutory transition; longer new service uses another status.

topics.title: Objecting to data transfer
topics.law: From 1 January 2026, the former military-information opt-out is repealed. SG §58c covers names and addresses of German citizens who turn 18 in the following calendar year; other privacy protections remain separate.

topics.title: Long stays abroad
topics.law: Since 17 April 2026, the general exemption removes individual applications and permission for foreign stays covered by WPflG §3(2). It does not remove unrelated travel or service duties.

topics.title: Leaving during probation
topics.law: FWD soldiers must request discharge one month ahead in the first five probation months. This request period does not apply in month six; discharge is still on the 15th or last day of a month.

topics.title: Truck licence subsidy
topics.law: For eligible first-time service entrants from 2026 who complete twelve continuous months, the first C/C1 licence can be acquired up to 36 months after service. The subsidy has separate cost and application conditions; class B uses twelve months.

topics.title: Discharge money
topics.law: FWD discharge money under WSG §8 requires more than six months of service, with specified exclusions. Exactly six months does not satisfy this threshold.

areas.title: Student finance
areas.intro: Federal grants and loans for students in Germany.
areas.publishers: Universities, student services and state portals

topics.title: Age limit
topics.law: Starting a qualifying Bachelor’s or Master’s phase before 45 satisfies the ordinary age condition. It does not establish the other BAföG conditions; specified age exceptions can apply from 45.

topics.title: Changing subject
topics.law: For a new undergraduate change, an established important reason can suffice before the fifth subject semester begins. Credited semesters, promptness and earlier changes matter; the Master route has a separate restriction.

topics.title: Earning while studying
topics.law: For ordinary employee earnings in a 2026 award period, an average €603 gross monthly is uncounted after standard deductions if no other income uses the allowance. This is not a universal gross-income limit.

topics.title: Savings and assets
topics.law: The basic allowance for applicant assets is €15,000, or €45,000 from age 30 at application. Parents’ own assets are not an asset input, although income from them can count.

topics.title: EU citizens who work
topics.law: Genuine EU-worker status can satisfy one BAföG residence condition. Twelve weekly hours are a regular indicator, not an absolute minimum; there is no categorical ten-week waiting rule. Other eligibility conditions remain.

topics.title: Second degrees
topics.law: One further qualification can qualify under narrow statutory exceptions. A medical graduate’s dentistry degree for oral and maxillofacial surgery is an identified special-circumstances example, subject to all requirements.

topics.title: When funding ends
topics.law: University training ends in the month successful completion is first notified, at latest the end of the second month after the final examination month. Payment still requires remaining funding duration and all other conditions.

topics.title: Spouses and children
topics.law: Qualifying childcare delays can justify an appropriate extension. A separate €160 addition to assessed need applies for each own child under 14 in the household, for one eligible parent. Parental independence does not itself exclude spouse income.

topics.title: Monthly rates
topics.law: A qualifying student living away from parents in the ordinary student health/care insurance category has assessed need of €992 before means testing. Other insurance categories and supplements can give different totals.

topics.title: Studying abroad
topics.law: BAföG has no general six-month advance-filing cutoff for foreign study. Funding starts no earlier than the application month and course start, subject to eligibility; processing can take longer.

areas.title: Basic income support
areas.intro: Jobcentre benefits for people who can work but do not earn enough to live on.

topics.title: Keeping part of your wages
topics.law: For ordinary employed claimants aged 25 or over, 30% of the gross monthly earnings slice above €520 through €1,000 is disregarded. Other earnings slices and eligible deductions are separate.

topics.title: When benefits start
topics.law: An ordinary living-cost application normally takes effect from the first of the application month. Payment still depends on eligibility for each day covered.

topics.title: Savings you can keep
topics.law: For a single 35-year-old whose approval period begins on or after 1 July 2026, the ordinary allowance against countable assets is €10,000. Other ages, separately protected assets, household allowances and earlier approval periods have different rules.

topics.title: Help with furniture
topics.law: A qualifying initial need for essential household equipment can arise after separation even if someone has had a home before. Ordinary replacement purchases are different; need, resources and any required move approval still matter.

topics.title: One-off support
topics.law: Specified one-off needs can qualify even when ordinary living costs are covered, if the particular need cannot be met. The Jobcenter may consider income for up to six months after the decision month; an unmet qualifying need and the other conditions remain necessary.

topics.title: Holiday jobs for pupils
topics.law: For pupils under 25 at general or vocational schools, earnings from employment during school holidays are excluded without a euro ceiling. Contractual training remuneration is outside this exemption.

topics.title: Upper age limit
topics.law: The SGB II upper age boundary depends on birth year. For the 1961 cohort it is the end of the month in which age 66 years and six months is reached. Other eligibility requirements remain; an old-age pension can exclude SGB II earlier.

topics.title: Repaying a deposit loan
topics.law: During continuing benefit receipt, the ordinary offset for a deposit loan is 5% of the applicable standard need per month, starting the month after payment and declared by written administrative act. Statutory offset exceptions and immediate-maturity situations are separate.

topics.title: Children’s activities
topics.law: Eligible children under 18 with qualifying participation costs receive a €15 monthly lump sum. Appropriate additional actual expenses can also qualify; this is not an unconditional payment to every child.

areas.title: Parental allowance
areas.intro: Federal payments for eligible parents caring for a young child.

topics.title: Changing your months
topics.law: Particular hardship can permit a change to an already paid life month. The overall benefit period and three-life-month retrospective limit still apply; Plus-to-Basis conversion is a separate exception.

topics.title: Premature births
topics.law: Birth at least six, eight, twelve or sixteen weeks before the medically certified expected date increases the shared Basis allotment by one, two, three or four months respectively. Other eligibility conditions still apply.

topics.title: Partnership bonus
topics.law: For the ordinary paired-parent bonus after a current birth, each parent must average 24–32 weekly hours in each of two to four concurrent consecutive life months. The other eligibility conditions still apply; qualifying sole parents have a separate route.

topics.title: Working while receiving it
topics.law: Ordinary work averaging no more than 32 weekly hours over the child's life month satisfies the working-time condition. This does not by itself establish entitlement; training and suitable day care have separate exceptions.

topics.title: ElterngeldPlus amount
topics.law: Plus is capped at half the hypothetical Basis entitlement without relevant post-birth income. With post-birth earnings, actual monthly Plus can equal actual monthly Basis; minimums, supplements and offsets have separate rules.

topics.title: Single parents
topics.law: The ordinary sole-parent route can include an adult child for whom Kindergeld or a child allowance is due. The other parent must live separately, and the tax-relief, income-reduction and other eligibility conditions remain.

topics.title: Both parents at once
topics.law: For ordinary current cases, concurrent Basis receipt is limited to one of the first twelve life months. Statutory exceptions cover specified premature births, multiple births and disability cases.

topics.title: Maternity benefit months
topics.law: Life months with entitlement to the specified maternity or insurance benefits count as Basis months. The child's life months govern, not calendar months or the date of cash payment; pre-birth periods and excluded maternity grants are separate.

areas.title: Visas and passports
areas.intro: Guidance from German embassies, consulates and town halls on visas, passports and ID cards.
areas.publishers: German embassies, consulates and town halls
areas.law: EU visa rules and German passport, ID card and citizenship law
areas.where: German embassies, consulates and town halls

topics.title: Visa deadlines
topics.law: Ordinary short-stay applications may be lodged within six months before travel, normally at least 15 calendar days beforehand; justified urgent cases can be lodged later. An admissible application normally has a 15-calendar-day decision period, subject to lawful extensions.

topics.title: Visa documents
topics.law: For an ordinary short-stay application, the recognised passport needs two blank pages, issue within the previous ten years and normally three months of validity beyond intended final Schengen departure. Insurance normally covers the intended stay. Statutory exceptions and protected free-movement families have separate rules.

topics.title: Who can apply
topics.law: The competent consulate normally examines applications from legal residents without a fixed six-month waiting period. Past overstay is assessed against current refusal grounds. Qualifying family members accompanying or joining a mobile EU citizen receive free and accelerated visa facilitation.

topics.title: Fees
topics.law: The ordinary domestic passport base fee is €70 from age 24 and €37.50 below 24; the adult €70 rate dates from 1 January 2024. Since 7 February 2026 the competent-mission supplement is €36. Ordinary ID base fees are €46/€27.60 plus €43 abroad. Extras and fee relief are separate.

topics.title: Passports and ID cards
topics.law: New Kinderreisepässe and extensions ended on 1 January 2024; this does not mean children cannot get ordinary passports. New ID cards normally require fingerprints from age six, subject to statutory impossibility exceptions. Legally capable applicants may apply personally from sixteen.

topics.title: Citizenship
topics.law: For foreign citizenship acquired on or after 27 June 2024, that acquisition alone no longer causes loss of German citizenship. Earlier acquisitions and other loss grounds require separate analysis.

areas.title: Air passenger rights
areas.intro: EU rules on compensation and care when flights are cancelled, delayed or overbooked.
areas.where: Flights leaving the EU, and EU airlines flying into it
areas.whereShort: Flights to and from the EU

topics.title: Compensation for late cancellations
topics.law: For cancellations notified 7–14 days ahead, the rerouting exception requires departure no more than two hours early AND arrival less than four hours late. A separate extraordinary-circumstances defence can also exclude compensation.

topics.title: Flights into the EU
topics.law: For an EU-carrier flight from a non-EU country into the EU, local passenger rules alone do not exclude EU261. The third-country exception requires an assessment of equivalent protection; proof of actual receipt is not always required.

topics.title: Refunds
topics.law: When Article 8 reimbursement applies, an already-flown part is refundable if the journey no longer serves its original purpose. The Regulation does not require that request to coincide with the unused-part claim; ordinary procedural limits still apply.

topics.title: Hotel and meals
topics.law: An eligible passenger involuntarily denied boarding and awaiting earliest rerouting is entitled to necessary hotel care. The replacement need not depart on a later calendar date.

topics.title: Long flights within the EU
topics.law: On intra-EU flights longer than 1,500 km, expected departure delays trigger basic care at three hours. Separately, the Article 7 rerouting reduction needs arrival no more than three hours late, including routes beyond 3,500 km.

topics.title: Compensation for delayed arrivals
topics.law: On a covered flight, arrival at least three hours late can trigger Article 7 compensation, subject to a proven extraordinary-circumstances defence. The amount for all intra-EU flights over 1,500 km and other flights between 1,500 and 3,500 km is EUR 400. A delay over three hours on those routes does not meet the Article 7(2)(b) reduction condition.
topics.provision: Regulation 261/2004, Arts. 5–7; Sturgeon, joined C-402/07 and C-432/07, paras. 61–63, 69

topics.title: Compensation reductions after rerouting
topics.law: For covered flights between 1,500 and 3,500 km outside the intra-EU category, Article 7(2)(b) allows compensation to be halved only when rerouting arrives no more than three hours late. Involuntary denied boarding isolates this rule from cancellation-notice exceptions.

areas.title: Mobile roaming
areas.intro: EU “roam like at home” rules for using your phone in other EU countries.
areas.where: Mobile customers in their home EU country

topics.title: Fair-use checks
topics.law: For the ordinary four-month presence-and-use test, both roaming indicators must predominate; either domestic indicator is a safe harbour. After an alert, changed use demonstrating domestic presence OR consumption can suffice. Separate abuse grounds have their own rules.

topics.title: Surcharges
topics.law: If fair use is exceeded, extra charges are capped. In 2026: €0.019 a minute, €0.003 an SMS, €1.10 a GB and €0.002 an incoming minute, before VAT.

topics.title: Your allowance abroad
topics.law: For eligible default regulated roaming, domestic benefits normally continue, subject to valid fair-use rules and the domestic off-net comparator. Open-data bundles have a price-based data minimum; per-unit prepaid credit has a different calculation.

topics.title: Monitoring and alerts
topics.law: The ordinary presence-and-use control needs at least four months of observation. Separately, customers subject to the default spending limit need an additional notice above €100 excluding VAT per monthly billing period, with data stopped absent the required response.

areas.title: Package travel
areas.intro: EU rules for trips that bundle flights, hotels and other services.
areas.law: EU Package Travel Directive, as adopted in each country

topics.title: Passing a trip to someone else
topics.law: A traveller may transfer a qualifying package to a substitute who meets its conditions, using the required durable notice. Seven days is sufficient under the cited national rules. Only reasonable actual transfer costs may be charged.

topics.title: Refund when the organiser cancels
topics.law: For the organiser cancellations covered here—too few participants or unavoidable extraordinary circumstances—all package payments must be returned within 14 days. Non-refundable supplier flights do not reduce that refund.

topics.title: Too few travellers
topics.law: For trips longer than six days, the low-participant-number exemption requires the contractual minimum and deadline plus notice at least 20 days before departure. Later notice loses that particular exemption; it does not automatically prove a damages award.

topics.title: Insolvency protection
topics.law: Under the Austrian PRV scheme, required insolvency protection includes accepted package funds even if acceptance broke the statutory payment restrictions. This does not establish any company’s actual guarantee or payout.

topics.title: Major changes to a trip
topics.lawKey: Rights depend on timing and severity
topics.law: A significant predeparture change can give a choice of acceptance or fee-free termination. During travel, termination depends on substantial nonconformity and the statutory remedy and alternative-arrangement conditions. Outside causes do not erase these rights.

topics.title: Claim deadlines after a trip
topics.lawKey: Two years, with prompt defect notice
topics.law: For German package contracts concluded from 1 July 2018, statutory defect remedies have a two-year limitation period from the contractual end of the trip. A separate one-month post-trip claim cutoff cannot reduce those rights. Travellers must still notify defects without undue delay; culpable failure limits price reduction and damages only to the extent it prevented the organiser from remedying the defect.

topics.title: Return transport after ending a disrupted trip
topics.law: If a qualifying package is terminated under BGB §651l for a substantial travel defect and includes carriage, the organiser must arrange equivalent return transport and bear its additional cost. Remedy deadlines and statutory exceptions matter. An extraordinary event alone does not establish this termination right.

areas.title: EU rail passenger rights
areas.intro: Company guidance on refunds, rerouting, compensation and assistance for rail journeys covered by EU rules.
areas.law: Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers’ rights and obligations
areas.where: Rail journeys within the EU, subject to service and national exemptions

topics.title: Money instead of vouchers
topics.law: Where EU delay compensation is due, the passenger can request payment in money. The statutory amount cannot be made voucher-only because the passenger lacks a Visa or Mastercard. Reimbursement after a qualifying cancellation may take the form of a sufficiently flexible voucher only if the passenger agrees. Voluntary voucher uplifts are separate.

topics.title: Choices after cancellation or delay
topics.lawKey: Expected final delay of at least 60 minutes
topics.claimKey: Choices narrowed by extra timing conditions
topics.law: If cancellation, a missed connection or departure disruption makes arrival at the contractual final destination reasonably expected to be at least 60 minutes late, the operator must immediately offer a choice of qualifying reimbursement, comparable continuation or rerouting at the earliest opportunity, or comparable travel later at the passenger’s convenience. A refund need not wait for alternatives to fail. The choice is not lost because a request follows the original departure time or a night train is less than 180 minutes late at departure. Expected arrival must allow for time the train can realistically recover.

topics.title: Costs of an alternative journey
topics.claimKey: No costs if arrival delay is under 60 minutes
topics.law: When the original disruption is expected to delay arrival by at least 60 minutes, Article 18 provides a choice of refund or continuation/rerouting. A carrier-authorised alternative, or necessary, appropriate and reasonable public rail/coach/bus transport booked after 100 minutes without rerouting information, can be reimbursable even if it gets the passenger to the destination less than 60 minutes late. The under-60-minute exception removes delay compensation under Article 19, not qualifying rerouting costs under Article 18.

topics.title: The minimum payment threshold
topics.lawKey: Threshold no higher than €4 per ticket
topics.claimKey: Boundary or currency rounding excludes valid payments
topics.law: Railway undertakings may set a minimum threshold below which delay compensation is not paid. The threshold may not exceed €4 per ticket, so an otherwise valid compensation amount of exactly €4 cannot be excluded. Conversion into another currency does not permit rounding the threshold upwards so that valid amounts worth more than €4 are withheld.

topics.title: Delays caused by infrastructure restrictions
topics.lawKey: Infrastructure acts do not erase compensation
topics.claimKey: No compensation for Adif speed limits
topics.law: For covered journeys, the EU minimum is 25% of the ticket price after 60–119 minutes and 50% after 120 minutes or more. Acts or omissions of the infrastructure manager do not qualify for the third-party exemption. A separate exception can still apply, including a delay disclosed before purchase or a qualifying extraordinary external event.

topics.title: Notice before disability assistance
topics.law: For covered journeys, a single notification at least 24 hours before assistance is needed satisfies Article 24(a). The temporary permission to extend that period to 36 hours ended on 30 June 2026. At a staffed station with trained staff on duty, timely notified boarding, transfer and alighting assistance must be ensured under Article 23(1)(e). Access rules, train and station accessibility, and timely arrival at the designated meeting point still matter. Adding a specially equipped carriage is a different service.

topics.title: Refunds and replacement travel during extraordinary events
topics.law: When disruption makes a delay of at least 60 minutes reasonably expected at the contractual destination, Article 18 gives a choice of reimbursement or comparable continuation/rerouting. The extraordinary-circumstances exception in Article 19(10) concerns delay compensation; it does not erase the Article 18 choices.

topics.title: When a retailer combines separate tickets
topics.law: Where a ticket vendor combines tickets on its own initiative in one commercial transaction and a connection is missed, Article 12(4) requires reimbursement of the transaction’s ticket price plus 75%. To escape that liability under Article 12(5), separate contracts must be recorded in a reproducible form and the passenger must also have been informed before purchase. The seller bears the proof burden.

topics.title: The delay needed for 50% compensation
topics.law: For an eligible covered journey, Article 19(1) sets minimum compensation of 25% of the ticket price at 60–119 minutes and 50% at 120 minutes or more. A carrier may grant more, but Trenitalia’s checked standard compensation also uses these bands. Its separate Frecce bonus for 30–59 minutes does not increase the 60–119-minute payment.

topics.title: Protection for connecting journeys
topics.lawKey: One transaction can cover several tickets
topics.law: For a connecting journey bought in a single commercial transaction from a railway undertaking, Article 12(3) treats a ticket or tickets as a through-ticket. The Article 12(5) exception requires both prior-purchase information and reproducible separate-contract information on the tickets or another document. The physical number of tickets alone does not decide protection.

topics.title: Refunds when a delay was known before purchase
topics.claimKey: Prior notice excludes the refund section
topics.law: Article 18(1)(a) retains the refund option where at least 60 minutes of arrival delay is reasonably expected against the still-applicable contractual timetable. Prior knowledge before buying excludes Article 19 percentage compensation under Article 19(9), rather than supplying a general Article 18 refund exception. A valid revised contractual timetable may affect whether the qualifying delay exists.

areas.title: Basic bank accounts
areas.intro: EU rights to a bank account for everyday payments, as implemented in each country.
areas.law: EU Payment Accounts Directive and national implementing laws
areas.where: Statutory basic payment accounts in the EU
areas.whereShort: Basic payment accounts in the EU

topics.title: Living in another EU country
topics.law: Consumers lawfully resident in the EU can qualify for statutory basic payment accounts across Member States. A bank’s local-residence condition must have a lawful national basis. Italy and Belgium give the relevant EU-resident right without requiring domestic residence. Identity, anti-money-laundering checks and enacted refusal conditions remain.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU Arts. 15–16; Italy TUB Arts. 126-noviesdecies–126-vicies; Belgium CDE VII.56/1, VII.57–59

topics.title: Eligibility for a standard account
topics.lawKey: A right to choose the basic account
topics.law: Maltese law gives qualifying consumers a right to a basic payment account. Being eligible for a commercial standard account does not itself remove that right. National genuine-interest, equivalent-account and anti-money-laundering conditions still apply.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU Art. 16; Malta L.N.258/2026 Reg.44; MFSA R.5.6.143–155 (applicable6 October 2026)

topics.title: Free accounts in Spain
topics.law: Since 28 December 2022, Spain’s ordinary income ceilings for free basic accounts are 3, 3.5 or 4 times the annual twelve-payment IPREM, depending on the family unit. Other statutory conditions and proof remain necessary.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU, Art. 18(4); Spain RD 164/2019, Arts. 2–4; RDL 20/2022, Art. 75

topics.title: Savings limits in Belgium
topics.law: Belgium permits an asset-based refusal where the relevant cumulative average annual credit balance exceeds the statutory ceiling, excluding the specified rental guarantees. The Royal Decree of 17 July 2024 raised the base amount from €6,000 to €10,000 from 1 December 2024 and introduced annual indexation. The official Gazette notice 2025009110 fixes €10,239.43 from 1 January 2026 under CDE VII.59 § 1 and § 2. Thus a balance above €10,000 but below €10,239.43 is not by itself this refusal ground. A qualifying lawful-residence status, no usable equivalent Belgian payment account (subject to closure notice), and AML/identity requirements remain necessary. This finding addresses savings balances only, not the separate treatment of consumer-credit contracts.
topics.provision: Belgium CDE VII.59 §§ 1–2; Royal Decree 17 July 2024, Arts. 1–3; Gazette notice 2025009110, effective 1 January 2026

topics.title: Notice before a basic account is closed
topics.lawKey: Two months for ordinary eligibility loss
topics.law: Termination for loss of the residence condition, inactivity exceeding 24 consecutive months, or a qualifying other Belgian account/balance ordinarily requires at least two months’ notice. Immediate effect is limited to the specified convictions within the last five years, intentional illegal use or eligibility-changing false information. Other legal duties and the statutory conditions for each ground remain relevant.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU Art. 19; Belgium CDE VII.59 § 2; Law of 20 April 2026 Art. 7 (effective 17 May 2026)

topics.title: Basic accounts beyond commercial markets
topics.law: German basic-account eligibility covers consumers lawfully resident in the EU. A bank’s ordinary supported-country list is not an additional statutory refusal ground. Statutory identity, anti-money-laundering, existing usable domestic account and other specified refusal grounds remain.

topics.title: Closing an inactive basic account
topics.law: In Germany, inactivity alone can justify terminating a basic account only after more than 24 consecutive months without an account-holder-initiated payment transaction, if that termination right was agreed, and with at least two months’ notice. Other statutory termination grounds remain separate.

topics.title: Transfers included in Portugal
topics.law: Portugal’s capped basic-account package includes 48 interbank transfers per calendar year through homebanking or the bank’s own applications. This expanded entitlement has applied since 27 August 2023. Additional services and transfers beyond the statutory bundle can have separate charges. ATM transfers and the separate third-party-app allowance have their own rules.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU, Art. 17; Portugal DL 27-C/2000 Art. 3(1)–(3), amended by Lei 24/2023 Art. 6; Art. 12(3)

topics.title: Portugal’s annual fee ceiling in 2026
topics.law: Portuguese law caps the annual combined charges for the statutory basic-account bundle at 1% of the Social Support Index (IAS). For 2026 the IAS is €537.13, so the cap expressed in cents is €5.37. A bank may charge less; the cap does not fix the bank’s price. Extra services outside the bundle remain separately chargeable.

topics.title: Notice before closing a basic account
topics.law: Loss of lawful EU residence can justify terminating a Maltese basic account, but this ground ordinarily requires at least two months’ prior notice with written reasons. Deliberate illegal use and eligibility-changing false information have separate immediate-effect rules; security, public-policy, failed-notice and other legal qualifications remain relevant.
topics.provision: Directive 2014/92/EU Art. 19; Malta L.N.258/2026 Reg.44; MFSA R.5.6.164–169 (applicable6 October 2026)

areas.title: Online shopping returns
areas.intro: EU withdrawal rights and related German rules for sending online purchases back, checked against German-language webshop guidance.
areas.law: Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU · German Civil Code (BGB)

topics.title: Opened packaging and examined goods
topics.law: For a German consumer’s distance purchase of ordinary goods, opening or losing the original packaging is not a general exception to withdrawal. Article 14(2) of Directive 2011/83/EU and BGB § 357a(1) distinguish the continuing right from liability for an actual loss of value caused by handling beyond what is necessary to examine the goods. German law also requires the prescribed withdrawal information before that liability arises. Specific exceptions remain, including genuinely unsuitable unsealed hygiene goods and unsealed audio, video or software, under Article 16 and BGB § 312g(2).

topics.title: Hygiene exclusions
topics.law: For ordinary online consumer goods purchases, withdrawal is generally available for 14 days. The hygiene exception requires goods genuinely unsuitable for return for health or hygiene reasons, supplied sealed, with that seal removed after delivery. A hygiene label alone does not remove the right, and an intact seal cannot trigger this exception. The CJEU also held that removing a mattress’s protective film does not by itself remove withdrawal rights. Other statutory exceptions, including genuine personalisation, remain possible.
topics.provision: Directive 2011/83/EU, Arts. 9(1), 16(e); BGB § 312g(1), (2) no. 3; CJEU C-681/17, paras. 34–48

topics.title: Time to send goods back
topics.law: For ordinary online goods purchases, consumers normally have 14 days after delivery to declare withdrawal. They must then send the goods back without undue delay and within 14 days after declaring withdrawal. Timely dispatch meets the return deadline; the trader need not receive them within that period.

topics.title: Refunding delivery charges
topics.law: After withdrawal from the whole online purchase, the trader refunds payments including the charge for its cheapest standard outbound delivery. The extra charge for a more expensive delivery option need not be refunded. Properly disclosed direct return postage can remain the consumer’s responsibility.

topics.title: Flat return-processing fees
topics.law: Exercising statutory withdrawal does not permit a flat administration or processing fee. Disclosed direct return costs may be payable, and compensation can be owed for actual diminished value caused by handling beyond what was necessary to inspect the goods, provided the required notice was given.

wehrdienst-ba-duration.claim: says service is six months of training plus one to 17 more months.
wehrdienst-ba-duration.quote: Er besteht immer aus 6 Monaten Grundausbildung zum Soldaten oder zur Soldatin und einer anschließenden Dienstzeit von 1 bis 17 Monaten.
wehrdienst-ba-duration.tr: FWD always consists of six months of basic training followed by another one to seventeen months.
wehrdienst-ba-duration.example: Someone interested in a six-month commitment may think it is not on offer, or sign up expecting up to 23 months in the same status.
wehrdienst-ba-duration.context: The page’s outgoing Bundeswehr career link now describes the current six-to-eleven-month range. That linked correction does not change the duration statement on the BA page itself. Pay, physical criteria and basic-training content were not adjudicated in this finding.
wehrdienst-ba-duration.scope: Scope: a new commitment in the statutory FWD status from 1 January 2026. SG §58b(1) permits six to eleven months; the first six are probation. The law does not guarantee that every applicant receives a particular offer. The duration change took effect on 1 January 2026 under Article 20(1) WDModG. The former provision applied before that date. No expiry of the new duration rule was identified at the access date. Transition: SG §101(1) preserves former §58b for soldiers already performing FWD on 31 December 2025. A continuing old-law commitment over eleven months is not unlawful for that reason. Section 101(2) provides a conditional application route into SaZ for certain old-law soldiers. Longer voluntary service remains possible under the separate Soldatin/Soldat auf Zeit (SaZ) status. The mismatch concerns the duration described for new FWD applicants, not a cap on every form of voluntary military service.

versions.quote: Er besteht immer aus 6 Monaten Grundausbildung zum Soldaten oder zur Soldatin und einer anschließenden Dienstzeit von 1 bis 17 Monaten.
versions.tr: FWD always consists of six months of basic training followed by another one to seventeen months.

wehrdienst-ba-national-overview-duration.claim: says voluntary service lasts 7 to 23 months.
wehrdienst-ba-national-overview-duration.quote: Der FWD dauert zwischen 7 und 23 Monaten
wehrdienst-ba-national-overview-duration.tr: FWD lasts between seven and twenty-three months.
wehrdienst-ba-national-overview-duration.example: Someone interested in a six-month commitment may think it is not on offer, or sign up expecting up to 23 months in the same status.
wehrdienst-ba-national-overview-duration.context: The finding covers this complete FWD accordion and its duration statement, not unrelated gap-year, pay or programme claims. wehrdienst-hessen-travel-permission.tr: The application must be made in good time before departure from Germany.
wehrdienst-hessen-travel-permission.example: A German man planning a year abroad in a situation covered by WPflG §3(2) could prepare an individual application that the current general exemption removes.
wehrdienst-hessen-travel-permission.context: The 4 February 2011 professional approval is visible. The 1 December 2025 technical modification predates the exemption and does not prove a legal update. Publication currentness rests on its continued catalogue offer, not a claim that the text was freshly written. The general exemption was checked in the original one-page Bundesanzeiger publication, not inferred from a simplified FAQ. The correct Foreign Office FAQ is retained as countercontext.
wehrdienst-hessen-travel-permission.scope: WPflG §3(2) contains a permission rule for covered men after their seventeenth birthday leaving Germany for more than three months, extending a permitted stay, or extending a previously permission-free stay beyond three months. The residence conditions and the statutory scope must be checked; this is separate from the readiness-questionnaire cohort. Using §3(2) sentence 5, the BMVg general order exempts all male persons otherwise subject to that permission requirement. Part I expressly removes any prior individual application or individual permission. The order was published on 16 April 2026 and became effective the next day, 17 April 2026, under part III. No fixed expiry appears in the checked order; it states the current position and may be changed in future. This is a general exception under the still-existing statute, not repeal of §3(2), a blanket exemption from every military duty or a promise about future emergencies. Ordinary registration and other independently applicable duties remain. No actual application, travel delay or official decision was observed. The current Foreign Office FAQ dated 20 April 2026 correctly describes the general exception. The Hessen entry’s 2011 professional approval and 2025 technical modification are disclosed; technical modification alone is not evidence of legal revision.

wehrdienst-unit122-probation.tr: a notice period of four weeks must be observed here
wehrdienst-unit122-probation.example: An FWD soldier requesting discharge during month six could think another four weeks are mandatory. That advance-request period does not apply, although discharge dates remain restricted.
wehrdienst-unit122-probation.context: The entire withdrawal answer and surrounding six-month timetable were read. The follow-on sentence says service may continue for up to six weeks; it contains no separate month-six qualification. This finding does not rely on an old three-month basic-training model. The guide itself uses six months of training. Its SaZ withdrawal paragraph is outside this finding.
wehrdienst-unit122-probation.scope: SG §58h(2) permits a written personal request during FWD probation for discharge on the fifteenth or last day of a month. The one-calendar-month advance-request requirement is expressly limited to the first five months. In month six that personal period does not apply. The current first-five-month distinction took effect on 23 December 2023 under the Act of 20 December 2023 (BGBl. 2023 I No. 392), Article 1 number 10 and Article 7. It predates the guide’s 8 December 2025 publication. No expiry was identified at access. The authority’s discharge order has a separate two-week notification provision. That is not a four-week personal request requirement. Written procedure, permitted dates and the actual service status remain relevant; this is not a promise of immediate departure on any day. Four weeks also differs from a calendar month. The confirmed proposition here is narrower: extending a fixed personal advance-request period into month six. It does not adjudicate the guide’s separate SaZ paragraph or other discharge grounds. Current central Bundeswehr call-up guidance and the January 2026 FWD flyer’s physical page 2 footnote correctly distinguish the first five months from month six. They are retained as same-publisher countercontext.

wehrdienst-bw-hub-truck-licence.scope: SG §31c requires a first voluntary service commitment with actual entry on or after 1 January 2026 and at least twelve continuous completed months of service. Signing a twelve-month commitment alone is insufficient. The first C/C1 acquisition must fall within twelve months before entry through thirty-six months after the end of service. Class B uses twelve months after service. The application deadline is separate: twelve months after both the qualifying service and acquisition conditions are met. Payment covers evidenced eligible actual costs, subject to the statutory rules against double funding and caps of €5,000 for C/C1 or €3,500 for B. The benefits are alternatives. This is not an advance or an unconditional payment promise. WDModG Article 3 number 6 introduced SG §§31b/31c; effective 1 January 2026 under Article 20(1), physical PDF pages 8–9 and 28. No expiry was identified. At 17 October 2026 the earliest qualifying twelve-month completions are still future; no existing recipient’s lost payment is inferred. The main hub directly links a detailed Bundeswehr guide dated 6 February 2026 which correctly distinguishes the 12- and 36-month acquisition windows. That countercontext does not change the hub’s unrestricted sentence.

wehrdienst-fwd-flyer-discharge-money.tr: €100 discharge money per month from six months of service.
wehrdienst-fwd-flyer-discharge-money.example: A person whose qualifying FWD lasts exactly six months could expect discharge money from the flyer. That duration fails the statutory more-than-six-month threshold; actual service dates matter.
wehrdienst-fwd-flyer-discharge-money.context: The retained quote follows visible PDF spacing. The narrow error is the inclusion of exactly six months, not the monthly €100 rate or taxation. The initial audit checked duration and withdrawal in this same flyer. The expanded pass separately adjudicated its discharge-money bullet; the earlier selected review was not a full legal certificate.
wehrdienst-fwd-flyer-discharge-money.scope: WSG §8(1) requires more than six months of service. Section 8(2) sets €100 per month of qualifying voluntary service with a Wehrsold entitlement. Exactly six months is insufficient; the finding does not require seven completed months. The more-than-six-month threshold was already in the WSG when it entered into force on 1 January 2020. It remains in the current law after the 2026 amendments. The new SG §58b minimum of six months took effect on 1 January 2026, making the distinction relevant within the flyer’s advertised programme. No expiry was identified. For calculation of the amount, WSG §8(3) excludes specified extension periods for inpatient treatment. Section 8(4) separately excludes specified discharge or removal cases from entitlement. Actual service entry and end dates, including SG §2(3) adjustments, can matter. No individual benefit calculation or assumed €600 loss is made. The finding concerns FWD with Wehrsold under WSG §1, not separate SaZ transition benefits. The flyer’s tax wording and other financial figures are outside this adjudication. Same-publisher March 2026 pay examples, physical page 2, correctly specify six months plus one day. The January flyer also correctly states the sixth-month withdrawal rule; checking that separate rule in the initial pass did not certify every benefit statement.

bafoeg-baf-01-02.scope: The 45-year limit applies from 1 August 2022 under the 27th BAföG amendment’s then-§ 66a(2). The Act was promulgated 21 July 2022; its general commencement was 22 July 2022. The age rule has its own application date. The former carryover for older approval periods in then-§ 66a(3) did not preserve the old § 10 age limit. No relevant current transition supports 30/35 or 44 as the ordinary limit for a new phase in 2026. At or after 45, § 10(3) sentence 2 Nos. 1, 1a, 1b, 2, 3 and 4 provides specified exceptions: entrance qualifications through certain later education routes, vocational admission, certain further training, an immediate qualifying Master, personal or family impediments, or qualifying new need after a major personal change. Prompt-start requirements apply to specified routes. Age is assessed at the start of the training phase; a birthday during that phase is not automatically disqualifying. Age 30 for parental-income independence under § 11(3) No. 2 is a separate rule. All other personal, course and means-test conditions still apply.

bafoeg-baf-02-02.scope: The 29th BAföG amendment changed the important-reason cutoff from the beginning of the fourth to the beginning of the fifth subject semester, and the first-change presumption from the third to the fourth. The changes took effect on 25 July 2024. BAföG § 66a(8) preserves former § 7(3) for changes or abandonments completed, or legally deemed completed, by the relevant semester start preceding 25 July 2024. Old cutoffs can therefore be correct for a specifically historical case. The examples here concern a new change in 2026. The new institution’s credited semesters are deducted when determining the relevant subject semester (§ 7(3) sentence 5). A first change before the fourth semester normally benefits from a presumption; later or repeated changes do not inherit that presumption. An important reason must actually exist, and changing promptly after recognising it matters. An unavoidable reason is a separate route. The important-reason route is excluded for a qualifying Master under § 7(1a) sentence 2. The change does not waive other funding requirements or guarantee a positive means-tested award.

missions-visa-four-week-cutoff.context:

missions-visa-passport-age-at-expiry.law: The ordinary issue-age test is issue within the previous ten years at application and separately at external entry. There is no general requirement to remain within that issue-age limit until visa expiry; the passport must still be recognised, valid and meet the separate validity margin.
missions-visa-passport-age-at-expiry.example: Hypothetical: a tourist has a recognised passport issued on 1 November 2016 and valid through 1 August 2027, enters on 25 October 2026 and leaves on 5 November 2026, with a visa expiring on 20 November 2026. The issue-age test is met at application and entry, and the validity margin is met; the website’s visa-expiry age test would nevertheless reject that document condition.
missions-visa-passport-age-at-expiry.context: [1] Federal Foreign Office / German mission; English: The full passport bullet separately requires two blank pages, a three-month validity margin and an issue-age test at visa expiry. The German counterpart instead gives a general maximum ten-year document age. This comparison concerns the point at which issue age is tested, not passport recognition, continuing validity or the separate age condition at entry.
missions-visa-passport-age-at-expiry.scope: The passport must be recognised, valid and meet the ordinary post-departure validity margin and blank-page conditions. An ordinary external entry after the ten-year issue-age limit is not made lawful by this finding. Emergency validity waivers and qualifying free-movement family rules require separate analysis. This is not a claim that every extended passport is recognised.

Tashkent’s wording calls for 22 insured days; the North Office’s separate wording calls for at least eight. missions-visa-insurance-extra-fifteen-da.context:
[1] German Embassy Tashkent / Federal Foreign Office; German: The insurance row appears in the mandatory document list and also specifies whole-Schengen coverage and at least €30,000. missions-visa-insurance-extra-fifteen-da.scope: Insurance must cover the actual intended stay throughout the required territory and meet the other Article 15 conditions; changed travel dates can require changed coverage. missions-missing-support-documents.quote: Applications with missing documents cannot be accepted.
missions-missing-support-documents.law: Article 19 sets formal admissibility conditions, including the form, passport, photograph, applicable biometrics and fee. missions-missing-support-documents.example: Hypothetical: an applicant with a valid form, passport, photo, applicable biometrics and fee, inside the filing window, lacks an employment letter. That may weaken the case or lead to a request/refusal, but is not by itself an Article 19 bar to lodging.

The list includes bank/employment and accommodation evidence, not just formal admissibility items. The parent HTML gives milder advice that incomplete applications may cause delay or refusal and permits further documentation. That context does not qualify the PDF’s categorical statement.
missions-missing-support-documents.scope: Missing Article 19 core elements can justify nonacceptance, subject to its humanitarian/national-interest/international-obligation exception. Applicable fee and biometric exemptions must be honoured. Necessary supporting evidence can still be requested and failure to establish a condition can justify merits refusal. Qualifying free-movement family applications have special rules.

missions-passport-validity-recommendatio.scope: Justified emergency waiver under Article 12(a); qualifying free-movement family-member rules require separate assessment. missions-visa-residence-wait.pub: Missions in Japan, Oman and Qatar
missions-visa-residence-wait.claim: require six months of residence before you can apply.
missions-visa-residence-wait.quote: have been here for less than six months
missions-visa-residence-wait.law: A genuine legal resident may apply to the competent destination state’s consulate for that district without a fixed six-month residence wait. Legally present nonresidents have a separate justified-application route.
missions-visa-residence-wait.example: Hypothetical: a visa-required worker who has legally moved to Japan two months earlier and genuinely resides there plans a German holiday. The passage sends that resident back to a previous country even though Article 6(1) contains no six-month waiting period.
missions-visa-residence-wait.context:
[1] German missions in Japan / Federal Foreign Office; English in Japanese navigation: In a list joined by “or”, the paragraph requires recently arrived, temporary or under-six-month applicants to apply at the mission of their previous residence. Lack of an appropriate permit is a separate condition. The current English visa index repeats the instruction and links this page.
[2] German Embassy Muscat / Federal Foreign Office; English: The answer first describes ordinary resident jurisdiction, then adds a completed six-month residence condition. A tourist visitor is not necessarily resident; the contradiction is confined to the separate newly legally resident scenario. The current English visa index directly links this FAQ. Its general legal-change disclaimer is preserved in the full source.
[3] German Embassy Doha / Federal Foreign Office; English: The full sentence limits non-Qatari applicants to residents with this length of legal residence, then permits immigration confirmation in addition to a QID. This general page expressly covers Schengen holidays as well as national visas; only the short-stay application condition is assessed here.
missions-visa-residence-wait.scope: A visit, entry stamp or short temporary presence does not automatically establish residence. Evidence of real legal residence and correct consular district is lawful. Germany must be the competent destination or representation must apply. Justified applications by legally present nonresidents are a separate Article 6(2) route; visa-free and free-movement cases require their own analysis.

missions-automatic-overstay-next-refusal.claim: says a past overstay without contacting the aliens authority before visa expiry automatically means the next visa will be refused.

missions-automatic-overstay-next-refusal.law: Past overstay alone is not a separate automatic-refusal rule. It may be decisive evidence in the individual assessment; an operative entry ban, refusal-of-entry alert or another statutory ground can require refusal.
missions-automatic-overstay-next-refusal.example: Hypothetical: a former visa holder who overstayed years earlier without the specified contact, has no current entry ban and now satisfies the stay allowance could read the FAQ as making any new holiday application automatically futile. The actual outcome must depend on the current statutory grounds and individual evidence.
missions-automatic-overstay-next-refusal.context: [1] German Embassy Kampala / Federal Foreign Office; English: The complete answer conditions this consequence on overstaying and not contacting the aliens authority in Germany before the visa expires. It then explains that timely contact allows that authority to examine extenuating circumstances for a possible extension. Neither sentence supplies an exception to the categorical next-visa consequence. The current visa hub directly links this FAQ; the current Schengen application page also refers applicants to it.
missions-automatic-overstay-next-refusal.scope: An operative refusal-of-entry alert or entry ban, an exhausted 90-in-180-day allowance, reasonable doubts about departure, or another applicable statutory ground can still require refusal. Past overstay is relevant evidence and may be decisive after individual assessment. Nationality or document exemptions may remove the need for a visa. Qualifying free-movement family members have special rules. Correct destination competence and consular jurisdiction must also be established.

missions-eu-family-insurance.law: Qualifying family members accompanying or joining an EU citizen exercising free movement receive entry-visa facilitation free of charge and as soon as possible. Ordinary tourist insurance and accommodation proof are not additional conditions on that route. Independent family visits and most visits to Germans in Germany require separate analysis.
missions-eu-family-insurance.example: Hypothetical: a visa-required spouse accompanying a French citizen on a two-week German holiday could read the checklist as requiring purchased travel insurance even after proving the relationship and joint travel. This example assumes both qualify under the Directive.
missions-eu-family-insurance.context:

missions-eu-family-insurance.scope: The applicant must actually qualify under free-movement law. Independent visits to a relative, most visits to a German citizen in Germany, extended-family facilitation cases, and stays beyond three months can require different analysis. Relevant returnee cases can engage EU rights. Abuse, fraud and permitted public-policy/security restrictions remain possible. A qualifying residence card may remove the visa requirement entirely.

missions-age-24-boundary.pub: Missions in Rabat, Pakistan and Podgorica
missions-age-24-boundary.claim: use the wrong age bands for document validity and fees.
missions-age-24-boundary.law: For ordinary passports and ID cards, the age at application determines the band: below 24 normally gives six years; age 24 and above normally gives ten. The lower fee band ends on the 24th birthday; an already issued document does not expire merely because its holder turns 24.
missions-age-24-boundary.example: Hypothetical: a 20-year-old choosing a 48-page passport in Montenegro could expect ten years instead of six, while a 40-year-old in Pakistan could expect an ordinary ID to last only six years instead of ten.
missions-age-24-boundary.context:
[1] German Embassy Rabat / Federal Foreign Office; German: The paired row uses >24 for ten-year validity and the full fee. The same age split appears for 48-page passports and ID cards. Current amounts are updated here, while the older linked leaflets also retain the boundary wording.
[2] German mission / Federal Foreign Office; German: The current table explicitly introduces the section for applicants aged 24 or older and lists the ordinary ID at €89 with six-year validity. The younger table also says six years. The potentially ambiguous passport six-to-ten wording is not used as another finding.
[3] German mission / Federal Foreign Office; German: The 48-page ordinary-passport row promises ten years below age 24. The adjacent 32-page younger row correctly says six years, and another current passport/ID article gives the correct age bands. The current Service menu nevertheless links this fee table.
missions-age-24-boundary.scope: The comparison concerns ordinary documents issued in the stated age band. Individual statutory restrictions, temporary passports, provisional or replacement ID cards and exceptional limited-validity documents require their own rules. Extra passport pages affect the fee, not the ordinary age-based validity period.

airlines-austrian-intra-eu-delay-care.quote: for four hours or more in the case of all flights of more than 3,500 kilometres
airlines-austrian-intra-eu-delay-care.law: On covered intra-EU flights longer than 1,500 km, an expected departure delay of at least three hours triggers reasonable meals/refreshments and two communications.
airlines-austrian-intra-eu-delay-care.example: An eligible passenger on an Austrian-operated intra-EU route above 3,500 km faces an expected departure delay of 3h30. The notice places that flight in its four-hour band; Article 6(1)(b) already requires meals/refreshments and two communications.

airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.claim: says compensation may be halved when rerouting on intra-EU flights over 3,500 km arrives up to four hours late.
airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.quote: no later than four hours after the scheduled arrival time for flights of more than 3,500 km
airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.law: The Article 7(2) rerouting reduction on intra-EU flights longer than 1,500 km requires arrival no more than three hours late.
airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.example: An eligible passenger is involuntarily denied boarding on an intra-EU Lufthansa-operated flight above 3,500 km. Rerouting arrives 3h30 late. Article 7(2)(b) does not permit a 50% reduction; the notice's distance-only paragraph does.
airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.context: Full notice reviewed. The preceding compensation amounts and the delay-care paragraph explicitly include the intra-EU category; the separate reduction paragraph omits it. Amounts table overlaps above 3,500 km, so do not assume an actual €200 payment or assert the carrier's applied amount. Narrowly allege an overbroad permission to halve the otherwise applicable Article 7 amount.
airlines-lufthansa-intra-eu-reduction.scope: Eligible involuntarily denied-boarding passengers offered rerouting on a Lufthansa-operated intra-EU journey above 3,500 km, arriving more than three but no more than four hours late. airlines-klm-third-country-scope.claim: makes local regulation alone an exclusion from EU rights on inbound EU-carrier flights.
airlines-klm-third-country-scope.quote: unless local legal regulation applies in that third country.
airlines-klm-third-country-scope.law: Article 3(1)(b), interpreted in van der Lans paragraphs 27–29, does not make any local regulation an automatic exclusion. The court requires an assessment of equivalent protection; actual receipt need not always be proved.
airlines-klm-third-country-scope.example: Hypothetical: An eligible passenger on a KLM-operated non-EU–Amsterdam flight faces a cancellation. The departure country regulates some air-passenger compensation, but equivalence of its purpose, eligibility conditions and implementation has not been established. Those local rules alone do not displace EU261.
airlines-klm-third-country-scope.context: Opening eligibility bullet checked together with the full cancellation, delay, denied-boarding and claims sections. Later references say local schemes may apply but do not qualify the blanket opening exception. The live legal-information hub links this notice, which in turn links the July 2021 PDF; both repeat the same scope condition.
airlines-klm-third-country-scope.scope: Only non-EU departures into the EU actually operated by an EU carrier, with ordinary eligibility met. Equivalent third-country protection can exclude EU261; this finding does not promise duplicate recovery or require proof of actual receipt in every case.

airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.src: Passenger Rights, general Air France/KLM notice, 2.2 Delay compensation
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.claim: publishes a general Air France/KLM notice permitting a 50% delay-compensation reduction by distance alone above 3,500 km.
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.quote: may be reduced by 50% for flights of more than 3500 km
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.law: Sturgeon paragraph 63 allows the long-flight delay reduction by reference to Article 7(2)(c), which excludes the intra-EU category. An intra-EU flight over 1,500 km arriving 3h30 late attracts the EUR 400 Article 7(1)(b) amount if otherwise eligible; distance over 3,500 km alone does not permit halving it.
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.example: Hypothetical: An eligible passenger on an Air France-operated Paris–Saint-Denis de la Réunion flight arrives 3h30 late for an ordinary operational reason. Both airports are within EU territory and the route exceeds 3,500 km. With no extraordinary-circumstances defence, Article 7(1)(b) gives EUR 400; the generic Air France/KLM notice published by KLM permits a 50% reduction despite Article 7(2)(b)’s three-hour limit being exceeded.
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.context: The opening eligibility conditions describe EU261 generally, and section 5 refers readers to Air France or KLM; the linked PDF also names both. The finding concerns KLM’s publication of that general notice for an Air France-operated journey. It does not assert that KLM operates Paris–Réunion. The cash table correctly puts all intra-EU flights over 1,500 km in band B at EUR 400, and the cancellation/denied-boarding footnotes use A/B/C categories. The delay footnote instead uses distance alone. Linked PDF physical page 4 repeats it; page 6 names Air France/KLM customer care. No actual payment is established.
airlines-klm-intra-eu-delay-reduction.scope: General EU261 notice published by KLM and referring to Air France/KLM, applied to an eligible Air France-operated intra-EU flight over 3,500 km arriving more than three and less than four hours late, absent a proven extraordinary-circumstances defence. Air France’s official summer 2026 network release establishes the Paris–Réunion route category; TFEU Article 355(1) places Réunion within Treaty territory. No KLM-operated route of this length within the EU is asserted.

versions.quote: may be reduced by 50% for flights of more than 3500 km

airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.src: EU Air passenger rights, compensation table for EU departures
airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.claim: lists a four-hour threshold for EUR 400 delay compensation on EU departures of 1,500–3,500 km.
airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.law: For a covered flight between 1,500 and 3,500 km arriving over three but under four hours late, Sturgeon paragraphs 61–63 and Article 7(1)(b) provide EUR 400, subject to ordinary eligibility and the extraordinary-circumstances defence. The separate table’s four-hour starting point conflicts with that rule.
airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.example: Hypothetical: An eligible passenger on a Qatar Airways-operated EU–Doha flight between 1,500 and 3,500 km arrives 3h30 late for an ordinary operational reason. No extraordinary-circumstances defence applies. The applicable amount is EUR 400, although the EU-to-non-EU delay table starts that amount at four hours.
airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.context: The Delays prose immediately before the tables correctly states a three-hour arrival threshold. The table specifically headed Compensation for departure (delays) – From an EU airport to a non-EU airport lists four hours for the 1,500–3,500 km row at EUR 400. This is a contradictory table, not a claim that the whole page or Qatar’s actual claims handling uniformly denies three-hour claims. The complete cancellation, denied-boarding and extraordinary-circumstances sections were also read.
airlines-qatar-eu-departure-delay-table.scope: Covered EU departures actually operated by Qatar Airways, journey between 1,500 and 3,500 km, final-arrival delay more than three and less than four hours, with ordinary eligibility and no valid extraordinary-circumstances defence. No allegation about Qatar-operated third-country–EU arrivals.

versions.quote: 4 hours or more

airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.src: EU Air passenger rights, cancellation or denied-boarding compensation table
airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.claim: shows half compensation for rerouted EU departures of 1,500–3,500 km arriving up to four hours late.
airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.law: Article 7(2)(b) allows the EUR 400 amount to be reduced to EUR 200 only when alternative-flight arrival is no more than three hours late on a 1,500–3,500 km journey. The table’s EUR 200 row extending to four hours is too broad.
airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.example: Hypothetical: An eligible passenger is involuntarily denied boarding on a Qatar Airways-operated EU–Doha journey between 1,500 and 3,500 km. Alternative transport arrives 3h30 late. Article 4(3) and Article 7 require EUR 400; Article 7(2)(b) does not permit the EUR 200 result displayed in the table.
airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.context: The prose above the table says compensation may be reduced according to two-, three- or four-hour distance bands but does not assign each band. In the Cancellation or denied boarding section, the EU-to-non-EU table explicitly assigns EUR 200 to the 1,500–3,500 km row at three to four hours. A later row shows EUR 400 from four hours, producing an overlap at exactly four; the example deliberately uses 3h30. The page separately states overall compensation of EUR 250–600.
airlines-qatar-medium-haul-rerouting-red.scope: Only involuntary denied boarding on covered Qatar-operated EU departures between 1,500 and 3,500 km, ordinary eligibility met, rerouted final arrival more than three and less than four hours late. Denial is not based on reasonable health, safety, security or documentation grounds. Voluntary surrender and cancellation notice exceptions are outside the example.

roaming-go-fair-use-or.claim: lets either time or use abroad trigger fair-use checks.
roaming-go-fair-use-or.example: An otherwise eligible active user spends 70% of the relevant days in Malta but makes 80% of usage while travelling in another EU state over four months. Those features do not correct the alternative ordinary tests. General terms give specific tariff/offer terms priority; current Smart terms refer back to the Product Terms for this policy. A plan-specific override could change an individual contract.
roaming-go-fair-use-or.scope: GO home customers using default regulated terrestrial roaming, with valid residence/stable links and no separate abuse indicator. Long SIM inactivity with mostly roaming use, sequential SIM use and organised resale have separate rules. No conclusion about every GO plan or actual enforcement.

roaming-cableworld-home-presence-require.tr: EU regulation requires you to spend more time in your country of residence than abroad within a rolling four-month window.
roaming-cableworld-home-presence-require.law: The ordinary four-month control observes presence and consumption cumulatively. Prevailing domestic consumption is a safe harbour even when domestic presence does not predominate; separate residence/stable-links requirements and abuse grounds still apply.
roaming-cableworld-home-presence-require.example: Hypothetical: an eligible Spanish-home periodic traveller has 70 days registered elsewhere in the EU and 50 days registered in Spain in the observed four months, but 70% of the relevant voice consumption occurs in Spain. With no separate abuse ground, domestic consumption prevents the ordinary warning/surcharge despite foreign presence predominating.
roaming-cableworld-home-presence-require.context: The permanent-use section first discusses more than four continuous months abroad and then gives a wider categorical explanation of EU law based only on home presence. The linked October 2026 tariff pack, physical pages 35 and 87, instead correctly states cumulative foreign presence AND consumption. This narrows the finding to the explanatory guide.
roaming-cableworld-home-presence-require.scope: Default regulated terrestrial EU roaming for normally resident/stably linked Spanish-home customers engaged in periodic travel, under the ordinary presence-and-consumption control. Excludes permanent relocation, failure to establish eligibility, SIM inactivity/sequential-SIM abuse, alternative tariffs and lawful sustainability derogations.

roaming-konecta-traffic-alone.law: Higher roaming consumption alone does not establish abuse under the ordinary four-month control. Prevailing domestic presence is a safe harbour. A mere continuation of some roaming after warning is also insufficient if changed use demonstrates domestic presence or consumption.
roaming-konecta-traffic-alone.example: Hypothetical: an eligible Spanish-home customer is registered in Spain for 85 of 120 relevant days but consumes 70% of the relevant data while on occasional EU trips. With no separate abuse ground, the domestic-presence safe harbour prevents an ordinary presence-and-use surcharge.
roaming-konecta-traffic-alone.context: The FAQ says higher roaming use over four months is excessive and extra charges can follow 15 days later if the customer keeps using the line abroad. It also allows residence documents. The full Orange-network terms are internally inconsistent: section 15 and SERVICIO EN ROAMING use single-indicator OR wording, while later CONDICIONES LEGALES ROAMING... item d correctly requires greater foreign consumption AND presence.
roaming-konecta-traffic-alone.scope: Customers with Spanish residence/stable links using default regulated terrestrial EU roaming during periodic travel; only the ordinary four-month consumption/presence control. Excludes separate SIM abuse, residence-proof failures and valid open-bundle volume limits.

package-exoticca-transfer.tr: No, you cannot transfer your trip to another person once purchased.

package-exoticca-transfer.context: Four languages share the same article ID. They are one repeated drafting family, not four independent errors. Non-English wording and translations were independently checked. No separate company copy of this specific sentence was established.

Spain requires at least seven calendar days; France normally requires at least seven-day notice unless more favourable terms apply. A substitute failing the trip requirements may be rejected. Airline reissue can be expensive. This does not guarantee free name changes or a change of destination/date.

rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.claim: Says there is no refund or reimbursement of costs when rerouting gets the passenger to the destination less than 60 minutes late.
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.quote: KEIN Anspruch auf Entschädigung, Erstattung oder Ersatz von Kosten […] die Verspätung bei der Ankunft am Zielort weniger als 60 Minuten beträgt
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.tr: No entitlement to compensation, refund or reimbursement of costs […] the delay on arrival at the destination is less than 60 minutes.
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.law: The quoted exclusion combines three different remedies. Article 19(9) does exclude the percentage-of-fare delay compensation when rerouting keeps the final arrival delay below 60 minutes. It does not withdraw the separate Article 18 right to qualifying alternative transport without extra cost or reimbursement of qualifying self-arranged transport. This finding concerns that overbroad exclusion of rerouting costs; it does not claim that an original ticket must also be refunded after the passenger completes the replacement journey.
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.example: Hypothetical: cancellation of an EU long-distance train means arrival at the contractual destination is expected to be at least 60 minutes late. The railway company authorises the passenger to buy a €40 replacement ticket with another transport provider under comparable conditions. That faster alternative gets them to the destination 30 minutes late. Article 18(3) requires repayment of the authorised €40 costs. The 30-minute final delay means no Article 19 percentage compensation; it does not remove the qualifying €40 cost claim.
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.context: The main passenger-rights page first promises compensation and assistance subject to the limitations below, links separate delay, cancellation and last-connection pages, then states the quoted blanket exclusion. Its English version repeats the exclusion. The directly linked cancellation/delay page separately and correctly promises necessary and appropriate alternative public transport costs if no onward-travel information is received within 100 minutes. That conflicting, more accurate guidance qualifies the finding but does not correct the main page’s express all-costs exclusion.
rail-oebb-rerouting-costs.scope: Published wording for qualifying long-distance journeys within the EU, including domestic Austrian long-distance and intra-EU international services. Excludes urban, suburban and regional services where national exceptions may alter individual remedies. The original disruption must satisfy Article 18 and the alternative journey must satisfy the authorisation or 100-minute information conditions; no finding about actual refusals or payments.

rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.claim: Says delay compensation is paid only when it is more than €4, excluding an otherwise valid amount of exactly €4.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.quote: Entschädigungen werden nur ausgezahlt, wenn der berechnete Betrag höher als 4 EUR ist.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.tr: Compensation is only paid if the calculated amount is higher than EUR 4.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.law: Article 19(8) permits nonpayment below a minimum threshold, and that threshold cannot be more than €4 per ticket. Exactly €4 is not below the maximum lawful threshold. FlixTrain’s passenger-rights page and §15.3 of its conditions both instead require more than €4; §15.3 explicitly attributes that rule to Article 19(8). The discrepancy is the boundary at exactly €4, not the lawful exclusion of smaller amounts.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.example: Hypothetical: a passenger pays €16 for a one-way FlixTrain journey entirely within Germany and reaches the ticketed destination 90 minutes late. Assume no Article 19(9) or 19(10) exclusion, no ticket-price refund and a valid timely request. The 25% minimum compensation is €4. Article 19(8) does not permit rejecting that €4 amount as below the payment threshold, but the published wording requires an amount higher than €4.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.context: The railway section of the rights page gives the 25% and 50% rates, lists compensation exclusions, then states the quoted payment boundary. The bus section begins only afterwards. The company’s current conditions refer readers to the rights page in §15.1 and repeat the more-than-€4 rule in §15.3 with a direct legal attribution. The homepage footer links both current pages. The conditions label the relevant clause approved 8 June 2023 and published 17 June 2023; current navigation establishes present availability, not a recent legal review.
rail-flixtrain-four-euro-threshold.scope: An otherwise valid Article 19 compensation claim of exactly €4 per ticket on FlixTrain long-distance services within the EU. The worked example is domestic Germany, where no long-distance Article 19 exemption is recorded in the Commission table. Other eligibility conditions and the exceptional-circumstances defence still apply.

rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.claim: Tickets and passes bought from 31 January 2026 earn no compensation when delay is caused by Adif’s temporary speed limits.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.quote: no generarán derecho a indemnización cuando el retraso se deba a estas limitaciones de velocidad.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.tr: will not give rise to compensation when the delay is due to these speed restrictions.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.law: The current page applies its exclusion to tickets and passes bought since 31 January 2026 because the infrastructure manager imposed temporary speed limits. Article 19 does not exempt an ordinary infrastructure-related delay merely because its cause lies outside Renfe. The mismatch is the blanket exclusion of the EU minimum. A passenger who was informed of the relevant delay before buying, or whose delay was directly caused by a qualifying external extraordinary event, may still fall within an exception.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.example: Hypothetical: a traveller pays €80 for a covered AVE journey affected by an ordinary Adif speed restriction of the kind described in Renfe’s notice and arrives 75 minutes late. Assume the ticket was bought after 31 January 2026, the passenger was not informed of the relevant delay before purchase, the ticket was not refunded under Article 18, and no Article 19(10) exception applies. The EU minimum is €20. Merely identifying Adif’s restriction as the cause does not remove that minimum.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.context: The opening notice and the final FAQ both state the exclusion. The FAQ immediately before it accurately refers to the Article 19(10) force-majeure grounds. The page discusses both current statutory rules and Renfe’s more generous punctuality commitments; it does not reserve the EU minimum when withdrawing compensation for speed limits. The captured site footer includes a current incoming link to this punctuality page. This records published wording, not proof of an actual refused claim. The current general conditions, effective 7 September 2026, state that compensation is due under applicable legislation, exclude passengers informed of the delay before purchase, and set higher 50%/100% bands subject to statutory exceptions. That correct contractual framing conflicts with the punctuality page’s unqualified speed-limit wording; this review does not establish which approach Renfe follows in individual claims.
rail-renfe-adif-speed-limits.scope: Limit to ordinary infrastructure operational restrictions within the set described by the notice, on covered Spanish services, and to the minimum EU right. Article 19(9) removes compensation when the passenger was informed of a delay before purchase, and Article 19(10) can cover an underlying qualifying extraordinary external event if its requirements are proved. No conclusion is drawn that every Adif restriction is compensable, that general news alone always suffices or never suffices as pre-purchase notice, or that Renfe must preserve every voluntary uplift. The Commission’s current table lists no Spanish exemption; it is an information table rather than an authoritative decision.
