rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.src: General transport conditions — scope of liability and compensation
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.claim: A purchaser without a Visa or Mastercard is told they cannot convert a refundable compensation voucher to money.
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.quote: Si el Comprador no dispone de ninguno de estos medios, no podrá recibir el crédito de su vale de compra reembolsable
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.tr: If the purchaser has neither of these means, they cannot receive the credit for their refundable purchase voucher
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.law: Section 3.2.2 requires Visa or Mastercard details to convert a refundable voucher into a card credit, and says that someone without either receives only a voucher for future direct bookings. Section 3.2.5.2 applies refundable vouchers to statutory delay compensation. Article 19(7) requires the statutory amount to be paid in money when the passenger asks. The company may set practical payment arrangements, but the stated absence of a card cannot erase the money option.
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.example: Hypothetical: a traveller who is also the purchaser holds a valid €80 paid OUIGO España ticket and arrives 75 minutes late. Assume a timely valid Article 19 claim, no Article 19(9) or (10) defence, no Article 18 refund, and that the purchaser has neither a Visa nor a Mastercard when requesting payment. They ask for money. At least the €20 EU minimum must remain payable in money; the published clause leaves only a future-booking voucher. This does not establish how the company would handle an alternative payment request.
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.context: The current conditions state an effective date of 21 August 2026. Section 3.2.2 applies the card condition to both direct and authorised-distributor bookings. Its next sentence leaves the voucher valid for direct bookings if neither card is available. Section 3.2.5 distinguishes compensation required by law from voluntary amounts and links the payment mechanism to both. The finding does not allege that every initial voucher is unlawful or that a voluntary voucher uplift must be paid in cash.
rail-ouigo-spain-compensation-card.scope: Only an eligible statutory delay-compensation amount under Article 19 is compared. Money is required on the passenger’s request, not automatically. Minimum-payment thresholds up to €4 and Article 19(9)–(10) eligibility exceptions remain applicable. No case of voucher-funded purchase, expired or already-used compensation voucher, or non-statutory goodwill payment is assumed. Spain has no listed applicable exemption. The research does not establish actual handling of a request for an alternative money payment method. The illustrated traveller is also the purchaser; the published card condition is addressed to the purchaser requesting conversion.

rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.claim: SNCF Connect describes a qualifying OUIGO cancellation reimbursement as payable only in a purchase voucher.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.quote: vous obtiendrez un remboursement intégral de votre billet OUIGO, en bon d’achat uniquement
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.tr: you will receive a full reimbursement of your OUIGO ticket, in the form of a purchase voucher only
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.law: For a covered cancellation that triggers Article 18(1), the passenger has the statutory reimbursement option. Under Article 18(5), reimbursement may take the form of a sufficiently flexible voucher only if the passenger agrees. The cancellation bullet instead describes the full reimbursement as voucher-only. This finding concerns the form of reimbursement; the separate cancellation-choice case concerns when that option is offered. OUIGO’s own FAQ allows eligible cancellation vouchers to be recredited to the payment account.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.example: Hypothetical: a passenger paid €80 by bank card for a covered France–Belgium OUIGO journey. The operator cancels the train and confirms that the replacement or exchange options described by SNCF Connect are unavailable. Assume arrival at the contractual destination is reasonably expected to be at least two hours late. The passenger has travelled no part, requests full reimbursement and does not agree to a voucher. Article 18(5) does not permit voucher-only reimbursement; the cancellation bullet describes precisely that payment form even after its own fallback conditions are met. No actual refusal or claim-handling practice is assumed.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.context: The statement appears under “Que faire en cas de retard ou suppression sur son train OUIGO ?”. After a 25%/50% delay scale and an automatic-voucher description, the cancellation bullets end with a full reimbursement “en bon d’achat uniquement”. The preceding sentence excludes reimbursement by bank transfer or physical cash; that wording alone does not exclude bank-card recredit and is not the basis of this narrowed finding. OUIGO’s own FAQ permits eligible cancellation and delay vouchers to be recredited to the original bank account, subject to its stated payment conditions.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.scope: Published SNCF Connect French guidance about a cancellation on a journey covered by Regulation (EU) 2021/782 where the Article 18(1) trigger is met. The example uses a France–Belgium international OUIGO service outside the local/regional exemptions, a wholly unused bank-card-paid ticket and no agreement to a voucher. It does not establish a general right to physical cash or a particular money-transfer method, and it does not allege actual refusals, losses or payment practice.

versions.tr: you will receive a full reimbursement of your OUIGO ticket, in the form of a purchase voucher only

rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.claim: SNCF Connect presents a cancelled-train refund as the fallback after a replacement or exchange proves impossible.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.quote: Si l’impossibilité se confirme, vous obtiendrez un remboursement intégral
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.tr: If that impossibility is confirmed, you will obtain a full reimbursement
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.law: For a cancellation causing an expected arrival delay of at least 60 minutes, Article 18(1) gives the passenger an immediate choice. Reimbursement under Article 18(1)(a) is available even when comparable continuation or rerouting is possible. The page instead orders the options as reallocation, exchange if that is impossible, and reimbursement if impossibility persists.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.example: Hypothetical: an eligible Paris–Brussels OUIGO service is cancelled and the next suitable train would arrive 90 minutes after the original arrival time. Assume the passenger has not travelled any part of the journey. They can abandon it and choose a full ticket reimbursement even though space is available on that later train.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.context: Under the cancellation heading, three successive bullets present reallocation, then an OUIGO-only exchange if impossible, and finally reimbursement. The refund method is a separate issue recorded in rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-voucher-only.
rail-sncf-connect-ouigo-refund-fallback.scope: Cancellation with a reasonably expected destination delay of at least 60 minutes on a covered service. This does not assert a statutory refund for every cancellation irrespective of the resulting delay. Wording only; no evidence of an actual refusal.

versions.quote: Si l’impossibilité se confirme, vous obtiendrez un remboursement intégral
versions.tr: If that impossibility is confirmed, you will obtain a full reimbursement

rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.src: Wheelchair services and current assistance-booking form
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.claim: Requires at least 36 hours’ notice for assistance on international rail journeys, although the EU extension allowing that period expired on 30 June 2026.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.quote: Takovou objednávku je třeba uplatnit minimálně 36 hodin před odjezdem vlaku.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.tr: Such a request must be submitted at least 36 hours before the train’s departure.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.law: The detail page says that including a foreign station activates the international assistance request, that it must be submitted at least 36 hours before departure, and that later submission cannot secure or guarantee the foreign partners’ service. Article 24(a) instead permits notification at least 24 hours before assistance is needed; its temporary national extension to 36 hours ended on 30 June 2026. For an otherwise eligible journey with trained staff, Article 23(1)(e) requires timely notified assistance to be ensured. This finding addresses the international-journey notice condition, not adding a specially equipped carriage or obtaining tickets through the assistance desk.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.example: Hypothetical: after 30 June 2026, a wheelchair user with a valid ticket for an already accessible ČD cross-border train from Czechia to Germany requests ordinary boarding and alighting assistance 30 hours before departure, more than 24 hours before the first assistance is needed. Assume available wheelchair capacity, accessible stations, trained staff on duty and timely attendance at the designated meeting point. The 24-hour EU notice condition is met; the published 36-hour international cut-off cannot turn that into a late request. No additional carriage or ticket-procurement service is requested.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.context: The current wheelchair-services page links the live booking form. The page first gives a 24-hour general notice period, then imposes 36 hours for journeys abroad and says later requests cannot be secured or guaranteed with foreign partners. Its actual booking form repeats 36 hours for travel abroad. The overview still says 48 hours for foreign travel, creating a further inconsistency; the finding uses the narrower 36-hour condition also present in the current form. The detail page separately says carriage may be arranged under immediate operating conditions without a prior order and preserves infrastructure, capacity and equipment limits. These qualifications do not change which notice period counts as timely for an otherwise eligible trip.
rail-cd-international-assistance-36-hour.scope: Ordinary disability/mobility assistance for an intra-EU ČD international journey after 30 June 2026, with Article 23 staffing and access conditions met. Czechia–Germany avoids Czech exemptions for services beginning or ending in certain third countries. Excludes adding accessible rolling stock, a five-working-day ticket-procurement service and any actual capacity/access barrier. Records public wording, not a demonstrated rejected request.

versions.tr: Such a request must be submitted at least 36 hours before the train’s departure.

rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.src: Current Conditions of Carriage, § 4.1(7) Czech / § 4.1(10) English
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.claim: Requires a free replacement-travel request by the original scheduled departure time, even in its section on delayed and cancelled services.
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.quote: must be exercised by the entitled passenger by the time of the regular departure time indicated on the ticket
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.law: The current conditions first give a refund or free rebooking when transport is not performed for reasons on Leo Express’s side, then say the free-rebooking request must be exercised by the scheduled departure time shown on the ticket. For a covered cancellation that triggers Article 18, that time limit cannot remove the statutory continuation/rerouting choice. A cancellation may be announced only after the original departure time; Article 18 still requires the operator to offer the choice and make arrangements. This finding concerns the specific original-departure deadline, not voluntary changes to an operating train.
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.example: Hypothetical: a paid domestic Czech Leo Express service is cancelled because of a mechanical failure ten minutes after its scheduled departure. Without replacement travel, arrival at the ticketed destination would be at least 60 minutes late. The passenger then asks for comparable continuation on the next suitable Leo Express train, rather than a refund. Article 18 requires that choice and the necessary arrangements; the conditions’ deadline has already passed before the cancellation was announced. The example does not assume the passenger can select any operator or fare without the applicable arrangements.
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.context: The live terms hub links the multilingual conditions identified as valid from 28 September 2026. The deadline appears in the dedicated delay/cancellation section, not in the voluntary cancellation section. It follows a six-month deadline for compensation/refund requests, making the distinct rebooking cut-off explicit. Czech and English repeat it with different paragraph numbering. The separately linked passenger-rights leaflet correctly describes continuation/rerouting at the earliest opportunity or later at the passenger’s wish, so it is retained as conflicting counterevidence. The contract generally states compliance with Regulation 2021/782; that does not explain the restrictive specific deadline.
rail-leoexpress-rebooking-departure-dead.scope: A covered Leo Express rail cancellation within the EU triggering Article 18, illustrated by domestic Czech travel and replacement travel requested after scheduled departure. Excludes voluntary passenger changes, Ukrainian bus legs and nationally exempt services. Does not claim both refund and replacement travel are due or establish actual refusal.

versions.quote: must be exercised by the entitled passenger by the time of the regular departure time indicated on the ticket
Nárok na bezplatnou přerezervaci jízdenky musí oprávněný cestující uplatnit do času pravidelného času odjezdu spoje uvedeného na jízdním dokladu
versions.tr: The entitled passenger must exercise the right to free rebooking by the scheduled departure time of the service shown on the travel document.

rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.claim: Its €4 minimum-payment threshold is converted to Swedish kronor and rounded up to the next ten kronor.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.quote: 4 EUR i SEK, avrundat uppåt till närmaste tiotal kronor. Detta belopp grundar sig på EU-förordningens bestämmelser.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.tr: 4 EUR in SEK, rounded up to the nearest ten kronor. This amount is based on the provisions of the EU Regulation.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.law: Section 15.3 converts €4 into kronor at the payment date and rounds the result upwards to the next ten kronor. Whenever the conversion is not already a multiple of ten, that makes the payment threshold higher than €4. Article 19(8) does not permit withholding an otherwise eligible compensation amount above €4 merely because it falls below that inflated threshold. The error is the threshold rounding, not the use of kronor for payment.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.example: Hypothetical, using an assumed exchange rate rather than a current market quotation: at payment, €1 equals SEK 11. The €4 cap is SEK 44; rounding it up makes the stated threshold SEK 50. A valid SEK 184 single ticket on a Stockholm–Göteborg long-distance train delayed by 90 minutes yields SEK 46 at 25%. That is worth more than €4 and must not be rejected under a SEK 50 payment threshold. Assume no Article 19(9)–(10) exception and no Article 18 ticket refund.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.context: Both current Swedish and English conditions repeat the upward-rounding rule and explicitly attribute it to EU provisions. They state entry into force on 9 October 2025. The live homepage links to the ticket-conditions hub, which links the Swedish conditions; its language switch leads to the English version. Both versions also contain a general mandatory-law savings clause. The English introduction still cites the former 1371/2007 Regulation; that obsolete citation alone is not a separate finding.
rail-vr-sweden-rounded-payment-threshold.scope: Otherwise valid Article 19 claims on covered VR Snabbtåg long-distance services. The illustration uses Stockholm–Göteborg, outside the Swedish exemption for domestic services whose total route is shorter than 150 km. The hypothetical rate is only for transparent arithmetic; no claim is made about today’s rate, actual processing, or rounding of an amount already being paid.

versions.quote: 4 EUR i SEK, avrundat uppåt till närmaste tiotal kronor. Detta belopp grundar sig på EU-förordningens bestämmelser.

rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.src: Rights in the event of a delay — night trains
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.claim: Its night-train explanation requires more than 180 minutes of departure delay before treating arrival as expected to be late.
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.quote: the delay at departure must therefore be more than 180 minutes.
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.law: Article 18(1) turns on a reasonable expectation of at least 60 minutes’ delay at the final destination under the transport contract. Recovery time may affect that forecast, but the law does not impose a separate rule that a night train must first be more than 180 minutes late at departure. The stated fixed requirement is too restrictive where the available forecast already establishes the statutory arrival-delay trigger.
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.example: Hypothetical: before departure of a covered Snälltåget night service within the EU, a passenger’s train is 120 minutes late at departure and a reliable operational forecast reasonably puts arrival at their contractual destination 90 minutes late, after allowing for time the train can make up. The passenger booked before the disruption and has not travelled any part. Article 18 requires the immediate choice of reimbursement or comparable continuation/rerouting; the departure delay being below 180 minutes does not postpone that choice.
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.context: The night-train paragraph follows the general statement that an expected final-destination delay of at least 60 minutes permits cancellation, rebooking or continuation. It explains that night trains may recover time, then adds the fixed more-than 180-minute departure requirement. Swedish and English versions match. The current FAQ, reached from the homepage, links this detailed rights page. The general transport conditions § 9.1 instead state the reasonable expected-arrival trigger without a 180-minute night-train proviso; that correct conflicting text is retained.
rail-snalltaget-night-train-180-minute-t.scope: Article 18 refund/rerouting choices on covered long-distance night services within the EU. A departure delay of 60 or 120 minutes alone does not prove eligibility: the reasonable arrival forecast must satisfy Article 18 after realistic recovery time. No finding about actual refused claims or the separate rules for compensation after arrival is made. Exclude Swedish domestic services whose whole operated service route is shorter than 150 km, and services outside the applicable EU scope.

versions.quote: the delay at departure must therefore be more than 180 minutes.
För att tåget ska beräknas bli försenat till slutstationen krävs därför en försening på mer än 180 minuter vid avgång.
versions.tr: For the train to be expected to be late at the final station, a delay of more than 180 minutes at departure is therefore required.

rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.src: Missed train connections in the EU
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.claim: Omio adds a force-majeure exception to the full-refund or free-rerouting promise for a single-ticket EU connecting journey.
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.quote: full reimbursement or a rerouting option at no additional costs (except in some cases, such as force majeure events)
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.law: The FAQ says that the same EU operator should guarantee a single-ticket connection by offering full reimbursement or rerouting without added cost, then excludes cases such as force majeure. Article 18 retains the reimbursement/rerouting choice when a delay of at least 60 minutes is reasonably expected, including in qualifying extraordinary circumstances. Article 19(10) can remove percentage delay compensation; it does not create the stated exception to reimbursement or rerouting.
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.example: Hypothetical: a passenger holds a DB through-ticket for Hamburg–Munich via Frankfurt. An extraordinary natural event causes a missed connection and a reasonably expected three-hour final delay. Even if DB proves the Article 19(10) compensation defence, the passenger retains the Article 18 choice of qualifying reimbursement or comparable continuation/rerouting. This does not guarantee a physically unavailable route or an immediate departure during an unsafe event.
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.context: The current dedicated FAQ displays an update date of 22 June 2026. The same clause is repeated in Omio’s current public disruptions campaign FAQ; these are one drafting family. The next sentence links to Omio’s general EU-rights article, which states the reimbursement/rerouting options without this force-majeure exception. Read that as counterevidence rather than suppress it. Direct original-byte requests returned HTTP 403, so retained captures are explicitly labelled selected web-tool transcripts, not original HTML.
rail-omio-through-ticket-force-majeure.scope: Genuine through-ticket and covered EU long-distance rail service with an expected final delay of at least 60 minutes. The example avoids regional exemptions and separate-contract disputes. Compensation and Article 18 reimbursement are different remedies. The relevant operator still makes necessary arrangements under comparable conditions, and timetable/safety realities may affect the offered routing. The claim concerns Omio’s explanation of carrier duties, not an asserted duty for Omio itself to operate replacement transport or evidence of an actual refusal.

versions.quote: full reimbursement or a rerouting option at no additional costs (except in some cases, such as force majeure events)
full reimbursement or a rerouting option at no additional costs (except in some cases, such as force majeure events)

rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.claim: Rail Europe says a separate-contract statement on tickets or another reproducible document removes the retailer’s refund-plus-75% liability, without also requiring pre-purchase notice.
rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.quote: This rule will not apply if this is clearly mentioned on the tickets […] that the tickets represent separate transport contracts.
rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.law: The article first describes the vendor’s reimbursement-plus-75% liability for tickets it combines on its own initiative in one transaction. Its following exception treats a separate-contract statement on the tickets or another reproducible record as enough. Article 12(5) makes two conditions cumulative: that record and information before the passenger bought. A statement first delivered with the tickets after payment cannot by itself remove Article 12(4) liability.
rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.example: Hypothetical: a retailer combines two covered long-distance rail tickets on its own initiative in a single €100 transaction. The customer is not informed before purchase that the legs are separate contracts; the tickets delivered afterwards clearly say so. The passenger misses a connection. Assuming Article 12(4)’s remaining conditions, the retailer owes the €100 ticket-price reimbursement plus €75 compensation. Clear post-purchase ticket wording alone does not remove that liability.
rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.context: The page identifies the EU Rail Passenger Rights Regulation and displays a 5 May 2026 update date. The exception is the last paragraph under What is a Combined ticket, immediately after the total-refund and 75% bullets. It is linked from the current missed-connection help article, which is itself listed in the Get help inventory; those links were followed. Direct original-byte requests were forbidden, so only accurately labelled selected web-tool transcripts are retained.
rail-raileurope-retailer-prior-notice.scope: Only vendor-initiated combinations in a single commercial transaction and an actually missed connection on covered services. The exception is effective where BOTH adequate pre-purchase information and reproducible separate-contract documentation are provided; the seller bears the proof burden. This is not an allegation about a completed Rail Europe booking or its actual notices. It does not turn every separately purchased ticket into a through-ticket or promise free rerouting as the Article 12(4) retailer remedy.

versions.quote: This rule will not apply if this is clearly mentioned on the tickets […] that the tickets represent separate transport contracts.

rail-trainline-trenitalia-sixty-minute-b.claim: Trainline’s Trenitalia table pairs a delay of 60 minutes or more with 50% compensation.
rail-trainline-trenitalia-sixty-minute-b.law: The table presents Trenitalia’s delay bands as 30–59 minutes for 25%, then 60 minutes or more for 50%. Article 19(1) gives a minimum of 25% at 60–119 minutes and 50% at 120 minutes or more, while allowing greater contractual compensation. The discrepancy is an inaccurate account of the checked standard Trenitalia scheme: its current guidance also uses 25% at 60–119 minutes and 50% at 120 minutes or more. Its separate 25% Frecce bonus for 30–59 minutes is non-cumulative and cannot be added to compensation for longer delays.
rail-trainline-trenitalia-sixty-minute-b.example: Hypothetical: an eligible passenger on a standard €80 Frecciarossa ticket arrives 75 minutes late and has not chosen an Article 18 refund. Assume no Article 19 eligibility defence and no special enhanced promotional arrangement. EU law and Trenitalia’s checked standard policy provide €20. The table’s 50% band suggests €40.
rail-trainline-trenitalia-sixty-minute-b.context: The article is dated 5 August 2024 and remains available at its original URL. The current robots-linked US CMS sitemap still lists that exact URL, but no recent editorial review is inferred. The caption introduces the compensation schedule for delayed trains in Europe; column headers are Train Company, Country, Delay Timetable and Compensation. Original HTML confirms parallel cells with 30–59/60+ and 25%/50%, with no up-to or maximum qualifier. Both the old carrier link in the row and the link in Trainline’s current operator-specific Help article target the same obsolete Trenitalia URL and return 404. The working current Trenitalia policy was independently located and read. Trainline’s linked general-rights Help article correctly states the EU 25%/50% bands; the operator-specific Help article does not repeat the erroneous band but its outgoing carrier link is broken.
rail-trainline-trenitalia-sixty-minute-b.scope: Limit to the table’s general Trenitalia 60–119-minute band and a covered standard journey. EU percentages are minima, so greater contractual compensation is lawful where actually offered; the checked current Trenitalia guidance is needed to establish this discrepancy. Frecce’s 30–59-minute voucher bonus is a separate voluntary right, not a cumulative extra 25%. A 120-minute-or-longer delay may qualify for 50%. This overstates a standard payment rather than establishing passenger harm, actual payout or intent.

versions.quote: Trenitalia […] 60 + Mins […] 50%

rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.claim: Says assistance abroad requires 48 hours’ advance notice.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.quote: Bei Hilfeleistungen im Ausland sind 48 Stunden Vorlauf erforderlich.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.tr: For assistance abroad, 48 hours’ advance notice is required.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.law: The page’s domestic recommendation is followed by a categorical 48-hour requirement for assistance abroad through Deutsche Bahn’s Mobility Service Centre. For covered intra-EU rail assistance, Article 24(a) permits 24 hours’ notice. Even the transitional national 36-hour option ended on 30 June 2026. The directly linked current DB page itself says 24 hours abroad. The discrepancy concerns the longer stated notice requirement, not a claim that BOB operates the foreign train or that assistance is unconditional.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.example: Hypothetical: after 30 June 2026, a disabled passenger who bought a covered Germany–Austria rail journey from the railway undertaking notifies that undertaking’s designated Mobility Service Centre 30 hours before the first assistance is needed. Assume a valid ticket, suitable access and equipment, trained staff on duty and timely presentation at the designated meeting point. This satisfies Article 24(a)’s notice condition. The BOB page’s foreign 48-hour statement incorrectly describes this timely notification as too late.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.context: The live BOB service menu links this page. It says its own trains have ramps and its drivers help with boarding, then directs readers to DB’s Mobility Service Centre for station assistance. The 48-hour statement follows a domestic recommendation to book by 20:00 the previous day. Its direct DB link now leads to guidance stating 24 hours abroad. This conflicting service-provider guidance is retained; no actual refusal or recent editorial review is inferred.
rail-bob-international-assistance-48-hou.scope: Published German company guidance about assistance on covered international journeys within the EU after 30 June 2026. Does not assess foreign services outside the Regulation, bespoke rolling-stock changes, or voluntary travel-planning extras. Article 23 staffing and access conditions remain necessary, and shorter-notice requests still attract reasonable-effort duties under Article 24(c).

versions.quote: Bei Hilfeleistungen im Ausland sind 48 Stunden Vorlauf erforderlich.
versions.tr: For assistance abroad, 48 hours’ advance notice is required.

rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.src: Passenger rights and responsibilities — connecting journeys on different tickets
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.claim: Its passenger-rights pages categorically treat connecting journeys on different tickets as separate contracts, without the single-transaction qualification.
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.quote: in virtù di differenti biglietti, i viaggi devono essere considerati distinti e separati tra loro
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.tr: because they use different tickets, the journeys must be treated as distinct and separate from one another
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.law: The Italian and English passenger-rights summaries first describe a single journey on one travel document, then categorically treat other journeys using different tickets as separate contracts. Article 12(3) covers one ticket or several tickets purchased in a single commercial transaction from a railway undertaking. Under Article 12(5), excluding that liability requires reproducible separate-contract information and notice before purchase. Different tickets alone do not satisfy that exception. The operative conditions contain conflicting terminology and a one-contract/multiple-titles clause; this finding is confined to the clearer website summary.
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.example: Hypothetical: a passenger buys two connecting covered Trenord regional services in one commercial transaction from Trenord and receives two tickets for a genuine planned connection with a reasonable scheduled change time. Assume no pre-purchase separate-contract warning or corresponding durable disclosure. The first train is delayed and the connection is missed, making arrival at the contractual final destination 90 minutes late. Article 12(3) engages the through-ticket protections in Articles 18–20; issuing two tickets does not by itself split the claim into unrelated contracts.
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.context: The current Italian and English rights pages repeat the categorical split and cite Regulation 2021/782. Their general May 2023 update label does not establish fresh editorial review. The linked current conditions hub leads to the original 102-page PDF effective 1 September 2026. Its Article 4 uses different titles rather than the websites’ different tickets. Printed page 8 defines title as a transport contract, and page 9 permits one contract to be formalised by one or more titles. Those clauses support a narrower interpretation of the PDF and are substantial counterevidence. The websites do not state the Article 12 single-transaction qualification. No actual booking or claim-handling practice was observed.
rail-trenord-separate-ticket-contracts.scope: Connecting journeys on covered services bought in one commercial transaction directly from a railway undertaking, where Article 12(5)’s information exception is not satisfied. Separate purchases, properly disclosed separate contracts, unconnected journeys and tickets merely gathered by a passenger are outside the example. This does not claim that every multi-ticket purchase is a through-ticket or that the three statutory remedies always produce a payment.

versions.quote: by virtue of different tickets, the trips must be considered distinct and separate from each other

rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.claim: Its terms extend the known-before-purchase delay exclusion to the full-ticket repayment in §9.1, although the statutory prior-notice exception concerns percentage delay compensation.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.quote: Resenär är inte berättigad till ersättning enligt punkt 9.1–9.3 om denne informerats om en försening före inköp av biljett.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.tr: A passenger is not entitled to compensation under points 9.1–9.3 if informed of a delay before purchasing a ticket.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.law: Article 18(1)(a) requires the reimbursement option where, at departure, arrival at the contractual final destination is reasonably expected to be at least 60 minutes late. For a journey not begun, choosing that option gives repayment of the unused ticket. Article 19(9) can exclude the separate percentage-of-ticket compensation when the delay was known before purchase; it does not add a prior-knowledge exception to Article 18. Section 9.4.1 expressly reaches §9.1, and the Swedish §9.1(2) itself calls full-ticket repayment ersättning, the noun used in the exclusion. The finding concerns that published monetary-refund cross-reference. It does not claim that all prior disruption information proves an eligible delay, or that a previously advertised arrival time must govern after a valid contractual timetable change.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.example: Hypothetical: a passenger genuinely buys a valid ticket for a covered Snälltåget long-distance EU service after being warned of a 90-minute operational disruption. The ticket and still-applicable published contractual timetable retain the original arrival time; no revised timetable is incorporated or accepted under § 3.4. At departure, a reliable forecast after recovery time still puts final arrival 90 minutes late. Before travelling any part, the passenger chooses to abandon the journey and asks for the ticket price back. Article 18(1)(a) retains that refund option despite prior notice. This assumes a genuine transport purchase and concerns neither percentage compensation nor private care costs.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.context: The exclusion is in the current general conditions. The Swedish §9.1(2) describes the full-ticket repayment using ersättning; §9.3 describes people remedied under §9.1 as compensated. The immediately following extraordinary-event exclusion is expressly limited to §9.3, whereas the prior-notice sentence names §§9.1–9.3. The English version uses refund in §9.1(2), but also describes §9.1 recipients as compensated in §9.3 and repeats the wider cross-reference. Material counterevidence remains: the introduction recognises mandatory law; the current delay page gives the ordinary expected-arrival refund choice and confines its prior-notice bullet to delay compensation; and §3.4 provides a mechanism for some preliminary timetable changes. The care-cost allegation has been excluded after the whole-subject review because its express reimbursement promise is in §9.4.2, outside the challenged cross-reference; this is a separately framed refund finding.
rail-snalltaget-known-delay-refund.scope: Published wording about the §9.1 monetary refund for a genuine covered transport contract, where the Article 18 expected delay remains at least 60 minutes against the still-applicable contractual/published timetable. Exclude a validly changed timetable producing no qualifying delay, Swedish domestic services whose whole service route is under 150 km, and non-EU services outside the applicable Regulation. Do not infer actual refusal, intent, universal booking practice, unconditional repayment after travel, care-cost exclusion or entitlement to both repayment and percentage compensation.

versions.quote: Resenär är inte berättigad till ersättning enligt punkt 9.1–9.3 om denne informerats om en försening före inköp av biljett.
versions.tr: A passenger is not entitled to compensation under points 9.1–9.3 if informed of a delay before purchasing a ticket.

banking-isybank-residence.claim: says its statutory basic account is only for residents of Italy.
banking-isybank-residence.quote: Il Conto di Base isybank, come tutti gli altri prodotti, è dedicato ai soli residenti in Italia.
banking-isybank-residence.tr: The isybank Basic Account, like all its other products, is intended only for residents of Italy.
banking-isybank-residence.law: Italy’s Banking Act gives consumers legally resident in the EU a right to a basic account regardless of where they live. Article 126-vicies permits refusal for the statutory eligibility and existing Italian payment-account grounds, subject to anti-money-laundering rules. Residence in another EU country is not itself a ground for refusal.
banking-isybank-residence.example: Hypothetical: A consumer legally resident in France, with no payment account in Italy, applies for a basic account and meets the identification and anti-money-laundering requirements. The published Italy-only restriction excludes that person even though living in France does not itself remove the statutory right.
banking-isybank-residence.context: The product page identifies this as the statutory Conto di Base and links it from the bank’s current account menu. Its application instructions also ask applicants to declare lawful stay in the EU. That broader declaration does not explain the page’s express Italy-only restriction; the linked information sheet dated 12 October 2026 repeats that account and card contracts are reserved for Italian residents (page 4). These are publications by the same bank, not independent drafting origins. The official Italian law capture is a March 2025 consolidation; the 2017 enactment and the regulator’s 19 August 2026 explanation were also checked. The live Normattiva article endpoint was unavailable. The Bank of Italy’s supervisory explanation published 5 August 2026 expressly confirms that the duty extends to lawful residents across the EU; its 30 November 2026 internal review deadline does not postpone the underlying statutory entitlement.
banking-isybank-residence.scope: Italian statutory basic accounts, reviewed on 18 October 2026. The right is for consumers legally resident in the EU and remains subject to identification and anti-money-laundering checks. An existing qualifying payment account in Italy can justify refusal, with switching and notice-of-closure exceptions. This is a finding about published eligibility wording; no actual application or refusal was tested. Standard accounts need not have identical conditions, and the basic account is not necessarily free.

versions.quote: Il Conto di Base isybank, come tutti gli altri prodotti, è dedicato ai soli residenti in Italia.
versions.tr: The isybank Basic Account, like all its other products, is intended only for residents of Italy.

banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.src: Cuenta de Pago Básica — vulnerability criteria
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.claim: uses income limits for a free basic account that were raised in December 2022.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.quote: ingresos inferiores a dos veces el indicador público de renta.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.tr: income below twice the public income indicator.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.law: Real Decreto 164/2019 Article 3(1)(a), amended by Real Decreto-ley 20/2022 Article 75 from 28 December 2022, sets ceilings of 3, 3.5 and 4 times the twelve-payment IPREM. Caixa Popular instead uses the earlier 2, 2.5 and 3 multipliers. The ordinary asset test, all account holders and authorised persons, application and proof requirements still apply. This is Spain’s enhanced fee regime under Directive Article 18(4), not an EU-wide income ceiling.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.example: Hypothetical: A sole holder, with no authorised persons and outside any family unit, has annual gross income equal to 2.5 times the applicable annual twelve-payment IPREM. Assume they meet basic-account eligibility, have no disqualifying property or company ownership and submit complete proof and an application for the fee exemption. Their income is within the legal 3-times ceiling but exceeds the page’s 2-times ceiling. No euro IPREM figure or guaranteed remedy is inferred.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.context: The current product page expressly makes the account free for vulnerability and then lists all four earlier income ceilings. It separately explains the asset test and the trafficking/sexual-exploitation route. The currently linked document labelled precontractual is a 2019 zero-fee information document headed Banco Cooperativo Español; it gives fees and does not correct the income criteria.
banking-caixa-popular-obsolete-free-acco.scope: Eligibility for Spain’s fee exemption for covered basic-account services. This finding does not treat vulnerability as necessary for opening the ordinary fee-paying basic account, and does not claim that all transactions outside the statutory service/quantity limits must be free. Published guidance only; no actual application decision, charging, harm or intent established. Selected sources do not establish a population error rate.

banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.src: Basic Payment Account · Who Can Open a Basic Payment Account?
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.claim: limits the basic account to people who are ineligible for a standard deposit account.
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.quote: You can only open a Basic Payment Account if […] and are not eligible for a Standard Deposit Account.
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.law: MFSA R.5.6.144 establishes eligibility for lawful residents of Malta or another Member State. R.5.6.146 permits genuine-interest checks, R.5.6.147 addresses an existing equivalent Payment Account with a closure-notice exception, R.5.6.148 prohibits refusal based on financial circumstances, and R.5.6.153 requires AML/CFT refusal. R.5.6.151 also prohibits burdensome restrictions dissuading exercise of the right. Eligibility for a commercial standard deposit account is not an additional exclusion from the basic-account right. These are the current 6 October 2026 Rules under L.N.258/2026 Reg.44, with repeal and transition in Regs.57–58; S.L.371.18 is historical.
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.example: Hypothetical: An adult legally resident in Malta has no equivalent Maltese payment account, needs ordinary daily banking and passes the required identity and anti-money-laundering checks. Even if BNF would accept them for its standard deposit account, that fact alone does not remove their right to choose the basic account.
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.context: The disputed sentence appears under the basic account eligibility heading. The linked April 2025 terms use EU/Member State residence and an equivalent-existing-account rule, including closure notice, without the standard-deposit-account condition. Those terms qualify any conclusion about the contract or actual processing.
banking-bnf-standard-account-eligibility.scope: Published basic-account eligibility wording in Malta. This review isolates a consumer legally resident in Malta with a genuine need and no equivalent Maltese account. The national genuine-interest, equivalent-account and anti-money-laundering conditions remain applicable. No actual application refusal or customer loss was established.

banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.src: Basisbankdienst · Voor wie is de basisbankdienst bestemd?
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.claim: still sets the savings ceiling at €10,000 instead of the indexed 2026 ceiling of €10,239.43.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.quote: u hebt bij een andere bank niet meer dan 10.000 euro schulden of gelden op rekening.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.tr: you have no more than €10,000 in debts or funds in an account at another bank.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.law: Belgium permits an asset-based refusal where the relevant cumulative average annual credit balance exceeds the statutory ceiling, excluding the specified rental guarantees. The Royal Decree of 17 July 2024 raised the base amount from €6,000 to €10,000 from 1 December 2024 and introduced annual indexation. The official Gazette notice 2025009110 fixes €10,239.43 from 1 January 2026 under CDE VII.59 § 1 and § 2. Thus a balance above €10,000 but below €10,239.43 is not by itself this refusal ground. A qualifying lawful-residence status, no usable equivalent Belgian payment account (subject to closure notice), and AML/identity requirements remain necessary. This finding addresses savings balances only, not the separate treatment of consumer-credit contracts.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.example: Hypothetical: An adult consumer lawfully resident in Belgium has no payment account in Belgium, no credit contracts and one Belgian savings account that does not provide the equivalent everyday payment services with a constant balance of €10,200 throughout the relevant year. The consumer satisfies identity and AML checks and all other statutory conditions. The average annual savings balance is €10,200, which exceeds the page’s €10,000 ceiling but is below the effective 2026 ceiling of €10,239.43; that balance alone cannot justify refusal.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.context: The product page introduces these as the conditions which must be met. Its current account-listing navigation links the statutory Basisbankdienst page. The directly linked information sheet dated 29 November 2024 also requires a cumulative average annual balance no greater than €10,000 (rental deposit excluded), calls these statutory conditions, and says Crelan will refuse if the conditions are unmet. The directly linked application incorporates that information sheet. Neither checked document states indexation of the asset ceiling.
banking-crelan-unindexed-asset-ceiling.scope: Finding restricted to Crelan’s published Dutch statutory-account savings guidance accessed 18 October 2026. No allegation about the separate credit-contract criterion, actual refusals, harm or intent.

banking-revolut-be-unindexed-asset-ceili.law: Belgium permits an asset-based refusal where the relevant cumulative average annual credit balance exceeds the statutory ceiling, excluding the specified rental guarantees. The Royal Decree of 17 July 2024 raised the base amount from €6,000 to €10,000 from 1 December 2024 and introduced annual indexation. The official Gazette notice 2025009110 fixes €10,239.43 from 1 January 2026 under CDE VII.59 § 1 and § 2. Thus a balance above €10,000 but below €10,239.43 is not by itself this refusal ground. A qualifying lawful-residence status, no usable equivalent Belgian payment account (subject to closure notice), and AML/identity requirements remain necessary. This finding addresses savings balances only, not the separate treatment of consumer-credit contracts.

The average annual savings balance is €10,200, which exceeds the page’s €10,000 ceiling but is below the effective 2026 ceiling of €10,239.43; that balance alone cannot justify refusal.

banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.src: De Basisbankdienst Rekening · Wat is een Basisbankdienst Rekening?
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.claim: contradicts its own EU-residence guidance by adding a principal home in Belgium as a statutory-account condition.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.quote: dat zijn hoofdverblijfplaats zich in België bevindt.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.tr: that his principal residence is in Belgium.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.law: CDE VII.57 § 2 grants the statutory basic banking service to consumers lawfully resident in an EU Member State; VII.56/1 prohibits nationality/residence discrimination and VII.59 sets the refusal grounds. A principal home in Belgium is not a separate condition. The Dutch product-page sentence expressly adds that condition even though the same page’s later eligibility list says residence in the EU. The linked July 2026 information sheet and French product version give the broader EU rule. The finding is this internal inconsistency in Dutch guidance, not a conclusion that Beobank’s whole application route or contract requires Belgian residence.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.example: Hypothetical: An adult French citizen lawfully resident in France wants Beobank’s Belgian statutory basic account for personal payments. They have no usable equivalent Belgian payment account, no disqualifying credit or savings balance, provide the required identity information, pass AML checks and meet all other statutory conditions. Their French principal home does not itself remove the Belgian statutory right, although the quoted Dutch sentence says the principal home must be in Belgium.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.context: The current Dutch account listing links the statutory product. Its introduction describes the legally regulated basic-account fee and expressly states Belgium as principal residence. The next eligibility list states that the applicant lives in the EU. The current French page has no Belgium-principal-home requirement. The directly linked original July 2026 information sheet expressly covers lawful residence in an EU Member State (and the statutory limited Belgian-national-abroad extension); the July 2026 application has no Belgium-home declaration.
banking-beobank-belgium-principal-reside.scope: Reviewed finding limited to the contradictory Dutch Beobank product-page statement. The nearby EU criterion, French text and linked July 2026 documents are material counterevidence. No actual refusal, bank intent or market-wide rate inferred.

banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.claim: contradicts its two-month notice clause by also listing loss of lawful EU residence as allowing immediate closure.
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.quote: zonder voorafgaande kennisgeving […] u niet langer legaal verblijft in een lidstaat van de Europese Unie;
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.tr: without prior notice […] you no longer reside lawfully in a Member State of the European Union;
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.law: CDE VII.59 § 2 permits termination on specified grounds. Where residence conditions cease (4°), inactivity exceeds 24 consecutive months (2°), or another usable Belgian account or a disqualifying balance exists (5°), termination of the framework contract requires at least two months’ notice. Immediate effect under this paragraph is reserved for 1° (the listed convictions within the last five years, or intentional illegal use) and 3° (eligibility-changing false information). The five-year limit was inserted by Article 7 of the Law of 20 April 2026, effective 17 May 2026. This comparison preserves the statutory Belgian-national-abroad residence extension and does not deny separate AML, sanctions, fraud-control or legally required payment/instrument suspension powers; the hypothetical excludes such a ground.
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.example: Hypothetical: A non-Belgian consumer’s lawfully opened Belgian basic account remains active and correctly disclosed. The consumer later ceases to meet the statutory EU-residence condition. There is no qualifying conviction within the last five years, fraud, intentional illegal use, misleading application information, AML/sanctions ground or other lawful immediate suspension requirement. Residence loss can justify terminating the account, but under VII.59 § 2 (4°) the framework-contract termination still requires at least two months’ notice.
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.context: The current Dutch contract lists loss of lawful EU residence under immediate closure/suspension. A following list in the same contract repeats residence loss under two months’ notice. Current English text has the same contradiction. This is an express contradictory notice rule in published contractual guidance, not evidence that Revolut has closed an account without notice.
banking-revolut-be-immediate-residence-t.scope: Reviewed finding concerning contractual framework-account closure for residence loss only, excluding operational suspension under other law. Same Revolut origin as the asset-ceiling case; not an additional independent publisher.

banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.quote: als u niet langer aan de toekenningsvoorwaarden voldoet, kan Beobank de rekening zonder voorafgaande kennisgeving opzeggen.
banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.tr: if you no longer meet the eligibility conditions, Beobank may terminate the account without prior notice.
banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.law: CDE VII.59 § 2 permits termination on specified grounds. Where residence conditions cease (4°), inactivity exceeds 24 consecutive months (2°), or another usable Belgian account or a disqualifying balance exists (5°), termination of the framework contract requires at least two months’ notice. Immediate effect under this paragraph is reserved for 1° (the listed convictions within the last five years, or intentional illegal use) and 3° (eligibility-changing false information). The five-year limit was inserted by Article 7 of the Law of 20 April 2026, effective 17 May 2026. This comparison preserves the statutory Belgian-national-abroad residence extension and does not deny separate AML, sanctions, fraud-control or legally required payment/instrument suspension powers; the hypothetical excludes such a ground.
banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.example: Hypothetical: An active Beobank basic-account holder truthfully notifies the bank that they have opened another usable equivalent Belgian payment account. The other account is not subject to a closure notice. There is no qualifying conviction within the last five years, fraud, intentional illegal use, misleading application information, AML/sanctions ground or other reason requiring immediate suspension. The new account can trigger termination under VII.59 § 2 (5°), but the framework-account termination requires at least two months’ notice.
banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.context: Footnote 3 follows the product-page eligibility list and says false declaration or any loss of eligibility permits no-notice termination. The French version makes the same broad statement. However, the directly linked July 2026 information sheet p. 2 expressly requires two months’ notice and limits immediate effect to the fraud/illegal-use/false-information cases. This case is the website’s broad notice statement only; the supplied contract information is contrary evidence.
banking-beobank-no-notice-eligibility-lo.scope: Reviewed finding limited to contradictory Dutch/French Beobank website guidance on notice. Same Beobank origin as the principal-residence case. No actual account termination, intent or harm inferred.

banking-n26-supported-country.src: Konto gemäß §§30 ff. ZKG — Why can’t I get a basic account?
banking-n26-supported-country.claim: says it may refuse the statutory basic account because the applicant lives outside its supported markets.
banking-n26-supported-country.quote: du außerhalb eines von uns unterstützten Landes lebst.
banking-n26-supported-country.tr: you live outside one of our supported countries.
banking-n26-supported-country.law: ZKG §31(1) gives each consumer lawfully resident in the EU the right to a German basic-account contract with an institution offering consumer payment accounts. §§32 and 34–37 limit additional conditions and refusal grounds; a commercial supported-market list is not among them. Existing usable domestic accounts, specified prior misconduct or lawful prior termination, and required identity and anti-money-laundering checks can still justify refusal.
banking-n26-supported-country.example: Hypothetical: An adult legally resident in Romania applies to N26 Bank SE for its German statutory basic account. Romania is absent from the linked supported-country list. Assume a complete application, successful required identification and anti-money-laundering checks, the ability to use the offered app services, no usable German payment account and no other statutory refusal ground. Romanian residence alone does not permit refusal, yet the FAQ lists unsupported-country residence as a reason to refuse.
banking-n26-supported-country.context: The German and English statutory-account FAQs expressly distinguish this product from N26 Standard. Their supported-country refusal bullet links a commercial country list that excludes several EU states. Current support-category navigation links the FAQ. The linked application accepts a country address field without listing supported markets; a separate current ZKG information PDF describes EU-wide entitlement and omits this market restriction. Those broader passages are retained as counterevidence. This concerns the express FAQ restriction, not a finding that N26 actually rejected applicants.
banking-n26-supported-country.scope: German statutory N26 basic-account guidance, checked 18 October 2026. The exclusion previously recorded for generic N26 ordinary-account criteria remains valid; this new finding uses the separate statutory ZKG page. Only published wording is assessed. No application, customer contact, refusal, harm or intent was tested.

banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.src: Basic-account application — background information, printed page 1
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.claim: says in its currently supplied application guidance that one year without turnover can justify closing a statutory basic account.
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.quote: ein Jahr lang umsatzlos geführt wird
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.tr: has been maintained without turnover for one year
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.law: Under ZKG §42(1), only the specified statutory termination grounds apply. For inactivity alone, §42(2)(1) requires more than 24 consecutive months without a holder-initiated payment, an agreed termination right, and at least two months’ notice. One year without turnover is insufficient by itself. Separate misconduct, unpaid-fee, false-information and other statutory grounds can still permit termination.
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.example: Hypothetical legal comparison: Assume the application guidance’s no-turnover condition is met for 13 months and there is no other statutory termination ground. That period alone is too short: ZKG §42(2)(1) requires more than 24 consecutive months without a holder-initiated payment. The example assumes the source condition is met; it does not equate bank-fee postings with no turnover or assume a particular N26 fee arrangement. Current contract terms separately incorporate the statutory rule.
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.context: The support FAQ currently links a nine-page application bundle whose first page identifies statutory ZKG basic-account background information and says the bank can also close an existing account when continuing it is unreasonable, including the one-year inactivity example. The current legal-document index independently links an eight-page application bundle with the same passage. Its legacy-looking device references are disclosed. Current 19 June 2026 interface terms 6.3 expressly incorporate §42(2) for basic-account customers; that correct contractual clause conflicts with the application guidance and prevents treating the one-year statement as proven operational policy.
banking-n26-one-year-inactivity.scope: Current linked German N26 statutory-account application guidance, reviewed 18 October 2026. Narrow published-information discrepancy only; no claim about actual closure, operative contract interpretation or all N26 publications. Same publisher/origin as the supported-country finding.

banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.src: Quais são os serviços incluídos numa Conta de Serviços Mínimos Bancários?
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.claim: contradicts its current terms by stating an annual included homebanking-transfer limit of 24 instead of 48.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.quote: existe um máximo, por cada ano civil, de 24 Transferências Interbancárias nacionais e na União Europeia.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.tr: there is a maximum, per calendar year, of 24 domestic and EU interbank transfers.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.law: Article 3(2) of DL 27-C/2000 includes 48 interbank transfers per calendar year via homebanking or the bank’s own apps within the capped package. Lei 24/2023 Art. 6 doubled the earlier 24 allowance; Art. 12(3) made it effective 90 days after 29 May 2023, on 27 August 2023. The FAQ understates the statutory bundle. The bank’s main product page, current FIN, DIC, general terms and statutory information document correctly state 48. The finding is limited to contradictory published guidance and does not establish charging or refusal.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.example: Hypothetical: a qualifying basic-account holder has made 24 ordinary euro interbank transfers through homebanking this calendar year and wants a 25th to an account in Portugal. Assuming no other issue affects the transfer, that 25th is within the statutory 48-transfer bundle. The FAQ’s 24 ceiling wrongly suggests it is outside. No claim is made that ActivoBank would charge: its current DIC prices ordinary online SEPA transfers at €0.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.context: The FAQ is listed under Serviços Mínimos Bancários in the current Contas help category. A separate paragraph on the current product page also puts homebanking transfers after 24 in the extra-services category, while the preceding included-services list says 48. Current product documents consistently give 48.
banking-activobank-obsolete-transfer-all.scope: Portuguese published explanation of the statutory bundle on 18 October 2026. One independent publisher; no actual charges, refusal, losses or intent inferred. Correct contractual and product material is material counterevidence.

banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.claim: gives €5.23 as the legal annual cap for 2026, although the 2026 cap is €5.37.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.quote: Em 2026 o custo anual dos serviços mínimos bancários não pode exceder 5,23€.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.tr: In 2026 the annual cost of minimum banking services cannot exceed €5.23.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.law: DL 27-C/2000 Art. 3(1) caps total annual charges for included services at 1% of IAS. Portaria 480-A/2025/1 fixes 2026 IAS at €537.13 effective 1 January 2026. One percent is €5.3713, expressed by Banco de Portugal as €5.37. ABANCA’s 5.23 figure understates that legal maximum by €0.14 at cent precision. A lower bank price is lawful; the page separately identifies its 2025 price, so this case concerns its explicit 2026 legal ceiling statement.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.example: Hypothetical: compare a full calendar-year statutory bundle priced at €5.30, with no separately chargeable extra services. In 2026, €5.30 is below the €5.37 legal ceiling. The page’s €5.23 ceiling would imply that price exceeds the law. This is an example of the numerical discrepancy, not ABANCA’s price or a recommendation.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.context: The quoted sentence appears under access and maintenance conditions, immediately after a statement that charges are limited by law to 1% IAS. The following sentence separately reports ABANCA’s 2025 annual price of €5.20 including stamp duty. Its currently linked FIN gives €2.50 plus 4% stamp duty per half-year, totalling €5.20. The currently linked DIC dated 1 April 2026 also gives €5.20 annually.
banking-abanca-portugal-obsolete-2026-fe.scope: Only the asserted 2026 statutory maximum on the Portuguese product page as accessed 18 October 2026. The bank may lawfully charge below the cap, and no excessive fee or harm is alleged.

banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.src: Basic Bank Account terms — section 5, Account Termination
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.claim: says it can close the basic account without prior notice when lawful EU residence ends.
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.quote: without any prior notification if: […] You are no longer legally resident in any EU Member State;
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.law: MFSA Rule R.5.6.164(d) permits termination when lawful residence in Malta or another EU Member State ends. R.5.6.168 requires grounds and justification at least two months before termination on that ground, free of charge and in a durable medium, subject to national-security/public-policy and failed-notice qualifications. Immediate termination under R.5.6.165 instead concerns illegal use and materially incorrect eligibility information under R.5.6.164(a),(c). L.N.258/2026 Regs.44,57–58 moved the governing rules and repealed the 2016 regulations; the MFSA Rulebook is applicable from 6 October 2026. Directive 2014/92/EU Art. 19 remains the EU framework.
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.example: Hypothetical: A customer truthfully opened a Maltese basic account, later moves to Canada and ceases to be lawfully resident anywhere in the EU. Assume no fraud, illegal use, sanctions, due-diligence failure or security/public-policy circumstance and that the customer can receive notice. The bank may close for loss of residence, but that ground alone does not allow closure without the statutory two-month notice. The customer receives and responds to communications; there have been no futile or rejected notice attempts.
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.context: The currently linked specific terms are effective from 1 March 2026. Section 5 puts loss of lawful EU residence under a no-prior-notification heading. A separate paragraph promises two months only for prolonged nil balance. The introduction says the specific basic terms take priority over conflicting other terms. The general terms also preserve statutory rights and discuss notice, which limits any inference about enforceability or actual processing.
banking-hsbc-malta-termination-notice.scope: Published HSBC Malta statutory basic-account terms only. The finding isolates notice where closure rests solely on loss of lawful EU residence. It does not challenge the availability of that closure ground or allege an actual immediate closure. Other legal grounds, security/public-policy qualifications and rules preventing unlawful account operation remain relevant. The separate rule for three futile or rejected notices does not apply to the hypothetical.
